activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
story:
The line outside the fire station moved in short, patient shuffles, and Sophia stood in it with her registration card going soft at the edges in her hand. Behind her, Marcus was still talking about the poll from Tuesday, the one he had screenshotted and sent to the group chat at midnight.

"Four-point lead," he said now, tapping her shoulder as if the number itself needed emphasis. "Margin of error is three. So even at the worst case, it's still a lead. It's basically over."

"It's not basically over," Sophia said. The man in front of them, older, in a coat too warm for November, glanced back and then returned to his newspaper.

"Three from four is one," Marcus said. "One is still bigger than zero. That's arithmetic, Sophia."

She had done that same arithmetic herself on Tuesday night, lying on her bed with her phone held above her face, and it had felt airtight, almost like a proof. She remembered the satisfaction of it, the way certainty had settled over her like a warm blanket. She had even typed a message to the chat saying the race was decided and it was pointless to argue about it anymore. She had never sent it. Something about the typing had slowed her down, the way copying a sentence slowly can transcribe doubt into a person, and she had deleted it instead and lain in the dark listening to the radiator tick.

The line advanced. Inside the station, the smell changed to floor wax and burnt coffee, and volunteers at folding tables called out street names in flat, unhurried voices. A woman with a lanyard checked Sophia's card, circled something, and pointed her toward a machine she didn't recognize from the diagrams she'd studied.

"First time?" the woman asked.

"First time."

The woman's smile was brief and genuine. "It goes faster than you think."

While Sophia waited for the machine, an argument caught her attention from the far table, where a younger poll worker in a hoodie was talking with a man holding a printed page. "You can't read it like that," the poll worker was saying. "The margin of error applies to each candidate's share, not to the gap. The margin of error for the lead is about twice as large."

Sophia stood very still. The words arranged themselves in her mind next to Marcus's arithmetic, and the arithmetic came apart. A four-point lead with a three-point margin of error was not a floor of one. Each share could move; the lead itself could move by more. She turned the idea over and could not make it sit still. Six, roughly, was the number for the gap, and six swallowed four whole.

"Marcus," she said quietly, when she was back beside him in the line for the stickers, "I think we had it wrong. The three points, it applies to each candidate's share. Not to the lead. The lead's margin is about twice as large."

He frowned at her, then at the gymnasium floor, the scuffed lanes of a basketball court visible under the folding tables. "Who told you that?"

"I heard it. Just now. And it makes sense of why I couldn't sleep Tuesday."

"You couldn't sleep over a poll?"

"I couldn't sleep because I was sure, and being sure felt too easy."

He didn't answer right away. A volunteer handed them stickers, the cheap kind, the adhesive already evanescent against her jacket sleeve, and Marcus pressed his onto his notebook like it was something to keep. She thought of her mother, who had once admitted, over dishes, that she hadn't voted in her first eligible election because the polls had said it was a landslide anyway, and who had refused, ever after, to tell anyone which election it was. The memory had always seemed like a small shame in the family. Now it seemed like something more complicated, a whole vote surrendered to a number that could not carry the weight assigned to it.

At the machine, Sophia made her choices. Her hand hovered longer than she had expected it to, not from indecision about the candidates but from the strangeness of the act itself, this private, unprovable moment that no poll had ever measured and no margin could contain. In her biology class they had spent October building a phylogeny of the hominids, tracing which fragments of skull descended from which, and she had learned that a tree of life is only as honest as its uncertainty, that scientists draw some branches with solid lines and some with dotted ones. The poll's dotted line had been the gap all along, and she had traced it solid.

When she came out, Marcus was waiting under the bare maple by the curb, breath fogging.

"So it could be losing," he said. It wasn't quite a question.

"It could be a lot of things. That's what the number actually says."

"It says less than I thought it did."

"Everybody says it says more than it does," Sophia said. She looked back at the fire station, at the line still stretching out the door into the gray afternoon, people waiting on the strength of numbers they mostly hadn't examined. Somewhere in that line was someone deciding not to bother, the way her mother once had. Somewhere in it was someone sure of an outcome the way she had been sure on Tuesday night.

"Then what's the point of polls?" Marcus asked.

She zipped her jacket higher. "They tell you where the fog is," she said. "They don't tell you what's inside it."

She started walking toward the bus stop, and after a moment, she heard his footsteps behind her.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Brody stood in the middle of the living room where the previous family had left faint rectangles on the carpet, and the movers had set his boxes along one wall in a line that looked like a small city seen from a plane. Somewhere outside, a sprinkler ticked across a lawn that didn't know him yet.

He found his phone in his back pocket and texted Marcus first, because Marcus would be awake even at ten in the morning on a Tuesday. "Landed. House is empty." Then he took a photo of the boxes and sent that too, because Marcus liked evidence.

The reply came in pieces, the way Marcus always texted, a thought arriving and then being corrected. "looks like a prison." Then, "of boxes." Then, "you find the kitchen yet."

Brody walked through the rooms to check. Kitchen: white counters, a window over the sink facing a backyard with one tree. He opened the fridge, which hummed at him like it was clearing its throat, and found nothing inside but a roll of quarters his mother must have left for the moving truck guys. He took two quarters and put them back. Even the small kindnesses in this house belonged to someone else's plan.

Upstairs, in what would be his room, he sat on the floor between two boxes and did the thing he'd been avoiding for the whole drive, which was to look at how many days of summer were left before school started. Twenty-six. Under that calculation sat a heavier one, the thing he'd read three nights ago at two in the morning in his old room with the walls already stripped of posters. He'd gone down a rabbit hole about making friends after a move, and one page had stopped him cold: a researcher named Jeffrey Hall, in a 2018 study, had estimated that moving from casual friend to friend takes about 90 hours together. Ninety hours. He'd lain there doing the arithmetic against the ceiling. If school was seven hours a day and you counted every minute, it would take almost thirteen school days, and nobody counted every minute, because most minutes you were just sitting near people, which didn't count, or did it, he didn't know, nobody had defined near.

He'd tried it out on Marcus before he left, sitting on the tailgate of Mr. Alvarez's truck while they loaded the last of the stereo equipment.

"Guess how long it takes to make a real friend," Brody had said. "Guess the hours."

"From nothing? Or from like, knowing the guy?"

"That's the thing, there's a difference. Casual friend to actual friend. This study says about 90 hours together."

Marcus had whistled, low, the way he did when a price came back higher than expected. "How long did we take?"

Brody had done that math too, lying awake. Six years of lunch periods, but you couldn't just multiply, because the first two years they'd barely spoken, and then the camping trip, and then junior year when Marcus's parents split and Brody had come over every day for a month without being asked. Whatever the real number was, it was enormous, and it was already spent, and that was what made it valuable and what made leaving feel like theft.

In the new room, he texted: "90 hours to make a real friend. im doing the math and its brutal."

"so skip casual. go straight to loyal," Marcus wrote back. Then: "join a club. same faces every week, it compounds."

Brody almost laughed at the idea of Marcus giving him advice, since Marcus's usual strategy in any new group was to become a sycophant to whoever seemed in charge, complimenting shoes and laughing at jokes that hadn't earned it, until he'd secured a position and could relax into being himself. It had worked, more or less, for years. Brody had watched it work and had never once considered it tenable for himself, not because he was nobler but because he couldn't act that well. The two of them had built their friendship on the difference, on Brody saying the flat thing and Marcus saying the smooth one.

The trouble was that now, in a town where he knew nobody, the flat thing felt like a luxury. You needed standing before bluntness read as honesty instead of hostility.

He got up and went downstairs, where his mother was taping labels onto cabinet doors so the unpacking wouldn't incapacitate her tomorrow, she said, when the fatigue hit. She had a system for everything. She looked up when he came in, and he could see her doing her own arithmetic, counting his silence like a bill coming due.

"There's a bike shop on Marsh Road," she said. "The sign said they're hiring. I know you didn't ask."

"I didn't ask."

"I know." She went back to her labels, then stopped, tape hanging off her thumb. "There's also a flyer at the grocery store. Some astronomy club, meets at the community college Thursdays. I took a picture of it, but I didn't sign you up for anything, I just. Took the picture."

He looked at the photo when she sent it to him, standing in the empty kitchen with the fridge humming behind him. Meets weekly, all levels, beginners welcome. Thursday nights from now until the school year ended. He counted the Thursdays out of habit, then counted the hours, three per night, and found the number was big enough to be a promise even though it was only arithmetic, and only about being in the same room.

He texted Marcus the flyer photo. Under it he wrote, "same faces every week."

He pulled his shoes back on, found his bike leaning against the garage wall where the movers had left it, and rode toward Marsh Road to see what a town he'd never chosen looked like at street level, the sun hot on the back of his neck, the flyer's picture still open on his phone in his pocket.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
story:
Hayden had waited until eighteen to learn to drive, which his mother said was sensible and his uncle said was cowardly, and the truth was neither, or both. He had put it off the way he put off dentist appointments, and then the summer before college had arrived with no more excuses in it. Now he sat in the driver's seat of the family Corolla in the empty lot behind the church on Delmar, his hands at ten and two, his mother in the passenger seat with her coffee held between her knees like something fragile.

"Foot on the brake, then start it," she said. He did, and the engine came alive under him, a vibration he felt in his teeth. He had imagined this moment for years, and in the imagining it had always felt like freedom, but the actual feeling was closer to being handed something heavy and breakable in a crowded room.

He let the car creep forward in the lot, turning wide, careful circles around the light poles. His mother adjusted the mirror on her side without comment, which he understood as a comment. When he braked too hard the second time, she set her coffee in the cup holder and said, "Smoother. Like you're setting it down, not catching it." He tried again and the car settled without lurching, and something in him loosened, and then immediately tightened again, because loosening was exactly what he could not afford.

They had been at the licensing office that morning, him filling out forms at a counter too low for his height. Two rows behind him, a girl about sixteen waited with her father for her permit test, reading a poster on the wall out loud to him in a bored voice. "Drivers aged sixteen to nineteen have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven," she recited, and then added, "Cheerful." Her father didn't look up from his phone. Hayden had copied the fact onto the back of his receipt without deciding to, the way you write down a phone number you don't trust yourself to keep.

In the lot now, circling, he thought about that number. Three times, per mile. He was eighteen, so he was inside the statistic, one of the counted, and the fact sat strangely with the confidence that was supposed to come from waiting, from being careful, from being the kind of person who read posters all the way through. His uncle's voice was in his head, saying the only way to get past it was miles, that caution this late was just fear wearing a costume. And his mother's was there too, quieter, saying nothing was worth the phone call at night. He had always let those two voices argue and stood apart from both of them, which had felt like wisdom and now felt like a stall.

"Take us out to Delmar," his mother said. "Real road. You're ready."

"Am I."

"That wasn't a question I was asking." She said it lightly, but her hand had gone to the door handle, and he understood that her body had made its own assessment. He signaled, checked the lot's exit, and pulled into the street, where the world stopped being a closed course and became other people, a man on a bicycle, a kid chasing a ball into a driveway, every one of them someone's whole life moving at speed past his windshield.

He drove at the limit exactly, which felt both tenable and absurd, like walking through a museum in a raincoat. At the light on Fifth he stopped early, and his mother laughed, a short sound, almost proud. "You know I totaled a car at seventeen," she said. "Your grandmother's Buick. A telephone pole. I paid her back for two years from the video store."

"Reparation," he said.

"Sweaty envelopes of cash, but sure." She was looking out the windshield, not at him, which was how she said serious things. "I'm telling you so you know the number on that poster is people. It was almost me."

He turned that over while the light held. Three times per mile, almost three times, for kids like the girl at the counter, like him, like his mother at seventeen with envelopes of cash. He could not make it mean don't drive, and he could not make it mean drive anyway and be brave, and maybe he would spend the next ten years finding where he actually stood, somewhere between his uncle's contempt and his mother's hands on the door handle. The light turned green. A horn sounded behind them, one short insistent note that seemed to presage the whole decade ahead of him, and his mother said, "Go," and he went.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
story:
The packing tables ran the length of the warehouse, and by half past four the October light through the high windows had gone the color of dishwater. Mackenzie had been stacking crates of canned peaches since seven, with forty minutes off at noon, and her hands knew the rhythm so well now that her mind had gone somewhere else entirely. It had gone to the meeting on Saturday, and to her father, who had said at supper that a man should be grateful for steady work and keep his mouth shut about the rest.

Ruth, who ran the second table, had not kept her mouth shut. She was older than the rest of them, maybe forty, with a son in Michigan, and she had spent two weeks collecting signatures on a folded sheet of paper she kept in her apron pocket. Mackenzie had watched her move down the aisle between tables, quiet as inventory, pausing at each woman's elbow. The word she used was union, said low, and the word she used after it was together, and some of the women signed and some looked at the floor and Mrs. Prue, the floor supervisor, developed a habit of appearing wherever Ruth happened to be standing.

That was Mackenzie's nemesis, if she was honest about it, though the word felt too grand for a squat woman with a clipboard. Mrs. Prue had cut Mackenzie's hours the week after her father complained about a short paycheck, and Mackenzie could never prove the two things were connected, which was somehow worse than a punishment she could name. She had learned that most unfairness arrived like that, in the shape of ordinary decisions that could each be defended on their own.

"Sixteen cents," said Dot, at the next table, not looking up from her crate. Dot was seventeen and had been there a year and a half. "Sixteen cents an hour, and Saturday they want us till nine again. I asked Mr. Hallis for eighteen and he said I was lucky to have the sixteen."

"My father says the same," Mackenzie said. "Lucky."

Ruth came down the aisle with her folded paper and, folded inside it, a scrap of newspaper she had been carrying since Tuesday. She laid it flat on Mackenzie's table, between two crates. It was a clipping from the front page, and Mackenzie read it slowly, because reading was still slower for her than lifting.

"October twenty-fourth," Ruth said. "Last Monday. There's a law now. The Fair Labor Standards Act." She tapped the page. "Took effect on the twenty-fourth of October, 1938. First federal minimum wage in this country, twenty-five cents an hour."

"Twenty-five," Dot repeated. She set down the can she was holding. "I'm making sixteen."

"And a maximum workweek of forty-four hours," Ruth went on. "Forty-four. That's the law, not a favor."

Mackenzie looked at the clipping and then at the clock above the loading door, and did the arithmetic twice because she didn't trust herself the first time. Sixteen cents against twenty-five. Fifty-two hours last week against forty-four. The numbers sat there, plain as weights on a scale, and she thought of her father saying lucky, and she thought of Saturday's meeting, which she had decided, that morning, to skip.

She had skipped things before. Two winters ago, when the girls at school had organized to confront a teacher who graded the boys more generously, Mackenzie had stood in the corridor while the others went in, and she had told herself she hadn't really agreed with them anyway, which was a lie she had maintained so long it had almost become true. Afterward the teacher's habits changed, slightly, for a term, and the girls who had gone in never quite trusted her again, and she had understood that there was a cost to standing in the corridor, only nobody billed you for it at the time.

"You can't just demand it," she said to Ruth. "Mr. Hallis will say he can't pay it. He'll say the company goes under."

"He'll say it," Ruth agreed. "But there's the law, and there's the lot of us, and there's what we can do together that none of us can do alone. That's what the meeting's for. Bargaining, when you're not alone." She didn't raise her voice. She never raised her voice, which Mackenzie had noticed was different from her father, whose opinions always arrived at full volume, gratuitous, like applause for himself.

Mackenzie looked down the row of tables, at Dot still holding her can, at the older women who had been there since before Mackenzie was born, at the clock that would not stop for any of them. She picked up Ruth's pencil, which was lying beside the clipping, and it was heavier than a can of peaches or lighter, she genuinely could not tell.

"Sign it," she said, mostly to herself, and then, louder, to Dot: "Twenty-five. Write down what you're making now, so we can show the difference."

Mrs. Prue came around the corner with her clipboard, and Mackenzie signed anyway.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Kaylee stood in her grandmother's doorway with a shoebox under her arm and the smell of cempasúchil already reaching her, dense and almost sweet, like the air itself had been instructed to guide someone in. Inside, the living room had been rearranged overnight. A table stood draped in white cloth, three tiers rising like steps, and on every tier marigolds, fresh-cut that morning, their orange so loud it seemed to argue with the candles.

"Put him at the top," her grandmother said, not turning from the kitchen. "With your mother's father. They got along, even at the end."

The shoebox held what Kaylee had rescued from her dorm room in September, when her father mailed it to her without a note: two photographs of her grandfather, a folded paper with his handwriting on it, and a small tin of the mints he used to carry. She had taken the box to college intending to do something with it, and instead it had sat under her bed for two months, going nowhere, until she came home for November first with a presentiment she could not name, the sense that if she didn't carry it to this table now, she would carry it unopened for years.

Her little cousins were already arranged around the altar like a tribunal. Paloma, who was nine, had appointed herself inspector. "You have to have marigolds," Paloma announced. "The bright color and the smell guide the souls home. That's the whole point. Otherwise he can't find us."

"He'll find us," Kaylee said.

"He can't. That's the whole point," Paloma repeated, with the finality of a customs officer.

Kaylee set the shoebox down and lifted out the first photograph, her grandfather in his work shirt, squinting into a sun she could feel through the paper. On November 1 and 2, her grandmother had explained once, years ago, families built these home altars, called ofrendas, and Kaylee had nodded the way children nod at things they assume will always be explained again later. Now no one was explaining. Her grandmother was ladling something in the kitchen, and her father had not yet arrived from the airport, and the task of deciding where her grandfather belonged on this table had fallen, without ceremony, to her.

The photograph of her mother's father already occupied the top tier, framed, surrounded by marigolds and a shot glass and a tiny guitar made of clay. Beside it was an empty stretch of white cloth. Kaylee hesitated there, photograph in hand, and found herself thinking about the funeral in the spring, which she had left early. She had told everyone it was a migraine. In truth something in her had gone torpid, a heaviness in her limbs that no weeping would move, and she had sat in the parking lot while they lowered him, furious at herself, and then not furious, just empty, and then furious again on the drive back to school. She had never told anyone she wasn't in the room when it ended.

She placed the photograph on the top tier, next to the other grandfather. Then she opened the folded paper, because keeping it folded on an altar felt like a lie. It was a grocery list, she discovered. Masa, piloncillo, batteries, and at the bottom, in his cramped hand, a note to himself: tell Kaylee about the well. She had no memory of any well. She stood holding a grocery list that had survived him and felt the loss double itself, once for the man and once for the conversation that now could not happen, and she could not decide whether putting the list on the ofrenda was reverent or strange.

"What's that?" Paloma asked, leaning in.

"A list," Kaylee said. "Things he meant to get."

"Put it down anyway. He might still want them."

Her grandmother appeared with a plate of pan de muerto and studied the arrangement over Kaylee's shoulder, saying nothing, which Kaylee had learned was her grandmother's form of approval. But her father's key sounded in the door, and Kaylee felt the old question rise before he even entered, the one she'd carried since spring: whether to tell him about the parking lot, or whether some failures are better left as private weather. He came in smelling of airplanes, hugged Paloma, looked at the altar, and stopped when he saw the photograph.

"You put him up," he said quietly.

"I did. Up top, with your father."

He set down his bag. Outside, someone's stereo started, and the candles bent in a draft from the kitchen. Kaylee smoothed the grocery list flat beside the photograph and said, before she could weigh it any further, "Dad, there's something I have to tell you about the funeral."

story:
The pan had been Grand-père's, and before that his mother's, though nobody in the kitchen could say anything about her except that she came from somewhere near Lyon and cooked with a violence Edouard had only heard described. He set it on the burner now, poured in a film of oil, and laid the chicken thighs skin-down, the way he had watched the old man do a hundred times without ever once asking why. The oil spat. The skin turned the color of parchment and stayed there, pale, sweating, steaming in its own juices while the kitchen window fogged over his father's newspaper on the table.

"You're cooking tonight," his father had said that morning, not quite a question, and Edouard had said yes, because in eleven days he would be in a dormitory three hundred miles away and this was the last dinner he could make in this kitchen. He had planned it for a week. Chicken, the potatoes from the bag on the back porch, the green beans his mother still bought at the same stall every Saturday because the vendor had known Grand-père. He wanted the meal to be good enough that his father would say something other than pass the salt. That was the whole want, and it embarrassed him, and he kept it anyway.

His mother came in at six with the beans and stopped at the stove. "It's not browning."

"I know." He pressed the thigh flat with the spatula. Water pooled and hissed and evaporated into more steam. The skin had gone gray, an obedient gray, cooked through and flavored by nothing.

"Turn it up, maybe."

He turned it up. Nothing changed that mattered. At seven he called them to the table anyway, because the potatoes were ready and his father did not like waiting, and they ate chicken that was moist and soft and completely without character, like something served to a sick person. His father ate three pieces without comment, which was its own sentence. Edouard pushed his own portion around the plate and thought about the funeral in March, where the priest had eulogized a man he had never met, some parish abstraction, while Edouard sat in the second row unable to stand up and say anything true.

He did the dishes alone. In the drawer beneath the dish towels he found Grand-père's grease-stained notebook, kept there since the apartment was cleared out, pages of lists and sums in a cramped hand. Halfway through, one page was different: temperatures. The pan must be much hotter, it said. Then, in French, then in English, as if he had been teaching someone: between 140 and 165 Celsius the browning goes fast. Amino acids and sugars. Maillard. Edouard read it twice and understood that he had been told this, probably, at eleven or twelve, standing on a chair at this same counter, and had not listened.

The next evening he took the last four thighs from the refrigerator an hour before dinner and left them on the counter, dry, unwrapped, because the page said dry. He set the cast-iron pan over the burner and let it sit, empty, while he trimmed the beans, and when a drop of water skated across the surface and vanished in a breath he laid the chicken in without moving it. The sound was different, a low sustained roar, and within two minutes the edges had gone the color of dark honey and were still going, and he thought: there it is, that was the whole distance, a hundred and forty degrees he had never bothered to want.

His mother had watched all of it from the doorway without speaking. She had come home early, hoping, she admitted to herself, to find the kitchen failed and empty so that the boy would feel free to leave on schedule, and instead he was standing over her father-in-law's pan with his sleeves rolled, and the smell in the room was the smell of every Sunday of her marriage's first ten years. She could not decide whether that was a gift or a small theft. The pan's provenance was muddled enough already: her husband claimed it, her son had inherited it in practice, and the woman from Lyon had presumably bought it for almost nothing at a market that no longer existed. It belonged to everyone and no one, an object out of its own time, anachronistic in a kitchen with an induction cooktop in the cupboard that they never used.

"Dinner," Edouard called toward the hall. "It's ready now, while it's hot."

His father came in and sat and looked at his plate for a moment before eating. The skin crackled. Underneath, the meat had kept its juice, and the flavor went deep, the way food had tasted when there were four of them at this table instead of three.

"The pan was hotter," Edouard said. "That's all it was."

His father took another piece of chicken, then a piece of bread, then, for the first time in Edouard's memory at this table, he reached across and served himself from his son's platter. "You'll want to take the notebook with you," he said. "It's yours, I think."

Edouard looked at the last thigh, golden, still ticking faintly in the cooling fat. "I'm not taking the pan."

"Then I'll hold it," his father said, "until you come back for it."

story:
Charlotte had been trying to draw her grandmother's hallway for three days, and it still looked like a child's diagram of a hallway, all doors and rug pressed flat against the paper like pressed flowers. She sat on the bottom step with her sketchbook propped on her knees, and the actual hallway stretched away from her, long and dim, narrowing toward the window at the far end. That was the part she could not get. The hallway itself did the thing; her drawing refused to.

Her grandmother came through with a load of laundry balanced on one hip and paused long enough to look over Charlotte's shoulder. "That's the hall, all right," she said, which was not the same as saying it looked like the hall, and they both knew it. She went on toward the kitchen, and Charlotte heard the washing machine begin its low churn.

She tried again. She drew the doors upright and parallel, the rug a long rectangle, the window a small square. Everything correct, everything wrong. The doorframes at the far end ought to be smaller, she could see that plainly when she looked up, but when she drew them smaller they seemed merely distant in a vague, floating way, unattached to the floor. She wondered whether the problem was in her hand or in her eye, whether she was drawing what she knew rather than what she saw. How would a person even begin to separate those two things?

In the afternoon she went looking for distraction and found her grandfather's study, a room she was usually circumspect about entering because of the model ships. On the desk, though, lay a paperback with a cracked spine, open to a page of diagrams. The book was about Florence, about the building of a cathedral dome, and Charlotte flipped through it without much hope until she reached a picture of a painted panel showing a baptistery so convincing, so present, that she turned the book around to see if the image changed. It did not, and yet it kept insisting it had depth.

She read the facing page twice. Around 1420 in Florence, a man named Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, a technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface. He had painted a view of a building and set it up so people could compare the picture with the real thing. She sat back on the carpet. Lines that meet. She thought of the hallway's ceiling edges and floor edges, how in her own eyes they ran toward each other the farther she looked, how the whole corridor seemed to lean inward around that far window. She had noticed it a hundred times without noticing it.

She carried the book to the bottom of the stairs, took out a ruler, and drew the hallway again. This time she put a single point in the middle of the paper, out where the window would be, and let every edge run toward it. The ceiling lines slanted down toward it, the rug's edges slanted up, the doorframes shrank along paths that all converged. When she finished, the hallway was there on the page, receding, holding depth in its flatness. She held the sketchbook at arm's length and compared it to the real hall until her grandmother's slippers appeared at the edge of her vision.

"What on earth are you doing sitting on the floor like that?"

Charlotte turned the page toward her. "It's called linear perspective," she said. "You draw the lines so they meet at one point, and it makes it look deep."

Her grandmother put on her glasses and studied it, tilting her head. "Well, that's the hall," she said, and this time the words meant exactly what they said. She tapped the far window with one finger. "That's where it all goes, isn't it. Everything heads for that bit of light." She went off to see about dinner, and Charlotte stayed on the step, looking from the drawing to the hallway and back.

There was something she could not quite settle, and she let herself not settle it. The trick worked because it lied so carefully, because a flat page could imitate the world only by pretending to be something it was not, lines that never truly touched in the hallway converging cleanly on her paper. And yet the hallway itself was honest, was simply there, and her drawing was honest about it in a lying way. Perhaps every drawing was a counterpoint like that, one truth set against another. Or perhaps she was overcomplicating it, and the hallway was a hallway and the drawing was a good drawing and dinner was at six.

In the kitchen the gravy had begun to coagulate where it sat too long, and her grandmother called for her to come stir it. Charlotte closed the sketchbook, keeping her thumb between the pages, and went.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
story:
The crystals were supposed to be the grandiose part. Logan's poster board, propped against the toaster, read The Hidden Architecture of Salt in block letters he now regretted, and beside it sat the jar of copper sulfate solution from which, after two weeks of patient evaporation, he had harvested a cluster of blue crystals weighing exactly 4.1 grams. The rubric wanted quantitative analysis. Mrs. Okonkwo had written "Where are your numbers?" in red pen at the bottom of his proposal, which was either a demand or a verdict.

He spread his notebook on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a bowl of bananas going soft at the stems. His little sister Priya sat across from him eating cereal with the concentration of someone watching television, except there was no television, only him.

"You're supposed to start from the mass of reactant," she said, milk dripping off her spoon. "I looked at your poster. It has zero numbers."

"Thank you. Extremely helpful."

He had dissolved 10.0 grams of copper sulfate pentahydrate in the water, and he knew from the side of the bottle that its molar mass was 249.7 grams per mole. He wrote it down, then divided, and got 0.0400 moles of the reactant. The reaction was a one-to-one affair, he was fairly sure, hydrate to anhydrous salt, so 0.0400 moles of copper sulfate should have come out the other end. He multiplied by the anhydrous molar mass, 159.6, and arrived at 6.4 grams. He sat back. Six point four grams was what the universe owed him.

The problem was the scale, which was his mother's kitchen scale, and the crystals, which weighed 4.1 grams. He weighed them again. He weighed the empty jar lid and subtracted. He weighed a banana, out of distrust, and got a number so reasonable it offended him. Two point three grams of copper sulfate had simply failed to appear, or had appeared and then failed to stay, and he had no idea which.

"Are you crying?" Priya asked.

"I'm doing math."

She came around the table and stood over his shoulder, which she did whenever she sensed weakness. "So how much did you get and how much were you supposed to get?"

"Four point one. Should have been six point four."

She tapped his notebook. "There's a thing for that. We did it in class. Percent yield. Actual divided by theoretical, times one hundred." She said it the way she said multiplication tables, bored and certain.

He wrote it down. Actual mass, 4.1. Theoretical, 6.4. He divided and got 0.64, carried the division out one more place to be sure, and multiplied by 100. Sixty-four percent. Sixty-four percent of the copper had cooperated; the other thirty-six percent was somewhere in the solution, still dissolved, or stuck to the string, or lost when he'd decanted the liquid into the sink because it had started to smell like the inside of a penny left in rain.

The question was what to do with the number. He could hide it, report only the moles, and let the poster stand on its hidden architecture. Or he could put sixty-four percent on the board in red, next to the crystals, and let Mrs. Okonkwo see that he had measured his own shortfall. His father would say a result is a result. His father also said that about parking tickets.

He looked up the etymology of "yield" on his phone while the kettle hissed behind him, because it felt like the kind of thing a good poster would include and because he wanted to know if the word had always meant surrendering something. It had roots in paying, in giving over. The crystals sat in their lid, blue and geometric, holding their 4.1 grams with what he was willing to interpret as dignity. In the corner, his mother's jar of sourdough starter sat fermenting on the counter, bubbling its slow argument with the flour, which had been going for three years now and which nobody had ever once weighed.

Priya leaned on the table. "Sixty-four's not terrible," she said. "Maddie's volcano did nothing. Zero percent. It just sat there."

"That's not a real yield. That's a lawn ornament."

He picked up the red marker and, on a fresh index card, wrote Percent yield: 64%, then held it against the poster, moving it from the corner to the center and back to the corner, trying to decide whether it was a confession or the most honest sentence he owned.

"Center," Priya said, and pointed her spoon at it. "Definitely center."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
Jayden's sister Thea had agreed to drive him to the airport only if he explained, before they reached the departures curb, what exactly he was doing in Japan for a year. He had forty minutes of highway left to figure out an answer that didn't sound like a brochure.

"It's an exchange," he said. "I go to school there. I live with a family. That's the whole story."

"That's the itinerary," said Thea, merging past a truck whose mudflaps declared it the property of someone named Duke. "The story is why. You turned down a summer program with your actual friends for this. I want the reasoning." She tapped the wheel twice, judge's gavel style. "You have until the parking garage."

The reasoning, if he was honest, was a diagram he'd seen in March and could not stop seeing: a population pyramid of Japan, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom, the exact opposite of the classic triangle his geography teacher had sketched to show a country full of children. Jayden had sat in that classroom feeling something rearrange. He had always thought of countries as fixed quantities, populations as weather, things you experienced rather than read. The pyramid suggested populations were architecture. You could look at the shape and know things. He'd looked up the number himself, late at night, half convinced he'd misread it: about 29 percent of Japan's people were aged 65 or over in the early 2020s, one of the oldest populations in the world. He'd checked it twice on two different sites, because a number like that felt like a rumor about the future.

"Okay," he said, digging out his phone. "Look." He held up the pyramid, top-heavy like a spinning top balanced wrong. "The bars are age groups. Men left, women right. Wide up here means lots of old people. Narrow down there means fewer kids. So if you're the government and you see this, you don't build the same stuff you built fifty years ago. You're deciding between schools and nursing homes. Whole towns with empty classrooms. That's the part that enraptured me, honestly, that you could predict a country's needs from one picture."

Thea glanced at the screen, then back at the road. "So you're flying nine thousand miles because of a bar chart."

"Because of what the bar chart means," Jayden said, and immediately wished he hadn't said means, because it invited the obvious question.

"Means how?" said Thea, obligingly.

He started to answer with the statistic, the clean 29 percent, the ranking, and then something snagged. The number was solid; it was everything around it that wobbled. "Here's my problem," he admitted. "I've got two ways of thinking at war in my head. Way one: the pyramid. It's basically arithmetic with ambitions. Wide top, old country, plan accordingly. Way two: the family I'm staying with has a grandmother. To the grandmother, the pyramid isn't a forecast, it's Tuesday. She's not a bar. And I can hold both of those in my head at the same time, but I can't make them shake hands yet." He drew the shape again on a napkin, adding a stick figure at the top, elderly, holding what was probably meant to be a cane or possibly a fishing rod. "I keep thinking about this village I read about, right on the coast, littoral, the kind of place where the school closed and the kids left and the beach is mostly herons now. On the pyramid that village is half a bar. In real life it's somebody's whole mailbox."

"Epistemology at seventy miles an hour," said Thea. "I did not agree to this."

"You literally asked."

"I asked for a reason, not a crisis." She was grinning, though, and she took the airport exit without signaling, which was her signature move. "So which is it? Are you going to be the kid who trusts the chart, or the kid who throws the chart out the window for the sake of one grandmother?"

"That's a false binary and you know it," Jayden said, but the question sat in his lap like the napkin. He looked at his sketch again. He didn't actually want to throw the chart out; the chart was why he'd applied in the first place, that vertiginous moment of realizing a picture could know a country's future. But he didn't want to be someone who mistook a shape for a population, either. Maybe, he thought, the position was this: the pyramid tells you what to expect and nothing about what it's like. He could carry both. He said so, out loud, and Thea said, "That's not an answer, that's a truce," and he said, "Truces are answers," and she pulled into short-term parking with eleven minutes to spare before he absolutely had to be at the check-in counter, deadline achieved by the ancestral method of running.

At the gate, backpack half unzipped, he texted her the napkin photo: the top-heavy pyramid, the ambiguous stick figure, and beneath it, in his cramped handwriting, "29% over 65. Will report from inside the bar."

Thea replied with a single heron emoji and, a moment later, "Go learn what Tuesday is like."

activity: graduating from high school
story:
Kevin stood at the edge of his own graduation party with a plastic cup of warm lemonade and watched his grandfather argue with a folding chair. The chair had collapsed under an earlier guest, and his grandfather, an irascible man who treated furniture as a personal adversary, was trying to force it back into shape while muttering in Portuguese. Kevin's mother had told him that morning to keep the peace, and he had spent the afternoon attempting to propitiate both sides of a family that had split along a fault line no one would name: the side that thought college was a sensible next step, and the side that thought Kevin was being stolen from them.

The diploma lay on the table beside the cake, still in its navy folder. His cousin Bruno picked it up first. "You're not even going to look at it?"

Kevin took the folder back, opened it, and frowned. The certificate sat flat inside, unfolded, corners sharp. "They didn't even fold it," he said. "That's the whole thing, apparently."

"The whole thing?"

"The word diploma. It's Greek. It means paper folded double." Bruno raised an eyebrow, and Kevin shrugged. "They used to fold official documents in half. That's where the word comes from. I found it out Tuesday, reading in the library instead of packing."

"So they gave you a folded-paper word for a flat piece of paper," Bruno said. "Congratulations."

Kevin's father appeared with the potato salad, set it down, and fixed on the folder with the expression he reserved for tuition statements. "You should frame it," he said. "Your tio Rui says Framingham State will take you in the spring, no debt, work at the shop until then. He's holding the position."

"He told me the same thing twice today," Kevin said. "Once with the position, once with the truck."

"That's not an offer you get twice."

Down the yard, his grandfather had given up on the chair and was instead telling Kevin's Aunt Lucia that the university had mailed them a bill for a dormitory Kevin had not yet seen. Kevin had heard two maxims from his father over the years, and the second one, delivered usually at the kitchen table over the bills, was that a man carries what his family gives him and nothing more. The first was that education is the one thing they cannot take back. He had never noticed until tonight that the two did not sit together comfortably, and that his father recited each with the same certainty.

He walked down to the table where his grandfather sat now, chair abandoned, and set the diploma folder in front of him. His grandfather opened it, ran a thumb along the embossed seal, and read Kevin's full name, including the middle name Kevin had tried to drop in ninth grade.

"Paper folded double," Kevin said. "That's all it is, word-wise. The Greeks folded the documents in half and the name stuck."

His grandfather looked at him for a moment. "Folded double. So it was small enough to carry in a coat."

"I never thought about that part."

"A man who carries his papers folded can run faster," his grandfather said, and closed the folder, and folded it in half himself, decisively, so the navy leather bent around the certificate. He set it back on the table like a completed transaction. "There. Now it is what it says it is."

Bruno caught Kevin's eye across the yard and mouthed, is that allowed? Kevin found he did not care whether it was. His father arrived at the table, saw the bent folder, and picked it up, and for a second Kevin braced for the argument, the two sides, the whole afternoon's careful diplomacy. His father unfolded it, looked at the crease running across the certificate, and then folded it back along the same line his grandfather had made.

"Tio Rui's holding the position until January," he said. "The dorm opens in September." He held the folder out to Kevin. "You can run fast either way, I suppose."

Kevin took the diploma and put it in the inner pocket of his jacket, which was hanging on the fence, which was where the dog was currently dragging it toward the hedge.

activity: going on a first date
story:
Brody arrived at the park eleven minutes early, which he decided he would spend looking casual, and which he in fact spent retying his shoes twice and rehearsing the phonetics of her name under his breath. Nadia. Three syllables, stress on the first, no mystery to it, but he mouthed it anyway like a spell that might fail if pronounced wrong. She had suggested the park over coffee, something about hating the acoustics of cafes, and he had said "totally" as though he had opinions about acoustics. He was standing now under an oak, one of a long arboreal line bordering the path, each tree dropping its seeds into the fountain with a faint plastic tick.

She came up the path with two paper cups, handed him one without ceremony, and said, "I didn't know what you take, so it's black and you can suffer." He laughed harder than the line deserved, then adjusted down to a normal laugh, and they started walking. The first ten minutes went fine. There was a dog wearing sunglasses. There was a man doing tai chi with a pool noodle. There was a goose that seemed to hold a grudge, though against what neither of them could say. By the time they reached the far end of the duck pond, the conversation had begun to thin, and Brody felt the silence coming the way you feel weather change.

"So," Nadia said, and then nothing followed it. He tried to propitiate the moment with a fact about geese, something he'd read about mate selection, and it landed wrong, possibly because he misremembered it, possibly because geese were not the point. She nodded politely. A seed ticked into the fountain behind them. He could feel the date sliding toward the parking lot, toward the polite text two hours later, toward nothing.

"Okay," she said, stopping on the bridge. "Can I try something? I read about this study once and I've always wanted to actually do it, and you're the closest available stranger." He said yes before she finished the sentence, which was either eager or honest, and she sat down on the wooden rail, cup balanced on her knee. "In 1997, this researcher, Arthur Aron, had pairs of strangers take turns asking each other thirty-six questions. The questions got gradually more personal as they went. And afterward those pairs ended up feeling closer than pairs who just made small talk." She looked at him to see if he thought it was stupid. He was already sitting down.

"That's the whole procedure? No eye contact ritual, no chanting?" "Just the questions. We take turns. And we answer honestly, which is the part I think people skip." She held up a hand as if she had the list memorized, though he suspected she was inventing. "Question one. Given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest?" He said his grandfather, who died when Brody was nine, and who he could no longer picture without a photograph, which he admitted was the actual answer rather than the charming one. She said a novelist she'd written a fan letter to at thirteen and never mailed.

The early questions were easy, almost silly, and they traded them like warm-up pitches while the goose patrolled below the bridge. But by the time she asked him to name the thing he was most grateful for in the last year, something had shifted; he found himself describing his mother's remarriage in more detail than he'd given anyone, including his best friend, including himself. He asked her about the perfect day and she answered with a day that had already happened, last October, alone, and then looked startled at having said it. "Interesting," she said, into her cup. "I didn't plan to say that."

They worked up through the middle of the list, where the questions stopped being clever and started being surgical. What friendship meant to each of them, said out loud, which turned out to be harder than having one. Whether there was something she'd dreamed of doing for a long time and why she hadn't done it. Brody gave his answer to that one and heard his own voice sound unfamiliar doing it. He noticed, somewhere in there, that he was both more himself and more constructed, that the closeness in the study was real and also something they were performing their way into, and he couldn't tell whether those were different things or whether it mattered. He decided it probably mattered and that he didn't care yet.

"Last one," Nadia said. The light had gone long and low across the pond, and the goose had given up on them. "Of all the people in your family, whose death would you find most disturbing." He took a slow drink of his terrible coffee. She watched him with her head tilted, waiting, and the fountain ticked behind them with its plastic seeds.

"My dad," Brody said. "Because I'd have to finish becoming someone without him watching. Your turn." She was quiet for a second, then laughed, not at the question but at herself. "I was going to lie," she said, "and say my grandmother. But it's my sister." She set her cup down on the rail. "Question thirty-six, or wherever we stopped. You get one more, and I get one more, and then I think they close the gates at dark."

story:
The folding chairs ran out before the cousins did, so Logan ended up on the piano bench in the corner of Aunt Rachel's living room, wedged between a stack of Haggadot and a bowl of pistachios. He had been to this Seder every year of his life and had never once had to do anything but eat and find the afikoman. That was the privilege, he was beginning to understand, of no longer being the youngest.

His cousin Sophie, seven, had that honor now, and she was hiding behind the ficus with a paperback Haggadah clutched to her chest like a wounded animal. When Logan brought her a plate of parsley, she looked up at him with wet eyes. "I can't do it," she whispered. "It's too many words."

"Do what?" he asked, though he already knew. He had watched his older brother, years ago, stand on a kitchen chair in this same room and recite in a voice that shook, and he had listened to his grandfather say, "The youngest asks the questions, that's how we begin." Nobody had explained it further. It was simply what happened, the way the youngest was always the one who had to ask why this night was different from all other nights.

"I have to ask the Four Questions," Sophie said. "In front of everybody. Aunt Mira already practiced with me twice and I messed it up twice." She opened the Haggadah to the marked page and turned it toward him, and there they were, printed in Hebrew above an English translation that began with the question he had heard every spring of his life: Why is this night different from all other nights?

Logan had an idea about how to learn things, formed mostly through cramming for chemistry exams: break it into pieces, then make the pieces into a rhythm. "Forget everybody," he told her. "Just do the first line for me. Quiet, just us." She swallowed and started, and her voice was so thin the words barely cleared her teeth, so he said, "Enunciate. Like you're telling a secret you actually want someone to hear." She tried again, louder, and a small astonished smile crossed her face when she finished the line without stumbling.

They worked through it in the corner for twenty minutes while the aunts argued over whether the charoset needed more wine and Uncle David told his annual story about the year he was impecunious and unemployed and someone's Passover dinner had been the best meal of his month. Sophie's brother Noah, home from his first year at college, drifted over at one point and began coaching too, but his method was all commands, tap the table on every syllable, chin up, project, and Sophie shrank with each instruction. Logan caught Noah's eye and tilted his head toward the kitchen, and Noah took the hint and went to bother the brisket instead. It occurred to Logan that there were two ways to get a kid through a performance: you could drill her like a soldier or let her discover she was capable, and he genuinely did not know which one his grandfather, who prized discipline, would call correct. Perhaps both, he thought. Perhaps it depended on the kid, which was a kind of discernment no rulebook could supply.

When Aunt Rachel dimmed the lights and lit the candles, Sophie's hand found Logan's sleeve and gripped it. The room settled. Grandpa raised his cup, and everyone leaned toward the youngest person present, who was still behind the ficus, and Sophie stepped out. Her shoes squeaked on the hardwood. She folded her hands in front of her like a news anchor, took the breath Logan had taught her to take, four counts in through the nose, and began.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?"

Her voice did not shake. It carried across the candles, across the folded chairs, all the way to the kitchen where Noah had gone, and Logan heard the pencil he'd been tapping go still. She asked about the matzah and the bitter herbs and the dipping, each question steadier than the one before, and when she finished, the whole table said the response together, a low rolling murmur Logan had never listened to properly until now. Sophie looked at him across the room and grinned, and Grandpa, wiping his eyes and pretending it was the horseradish, said, "Sophie, sweetheart, you may sit. Somebody pour this girl some grape juice."

Logan slipped her the first cup himself.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
story:
Kate came to the library every Tuesday to escape the noise of the cafeteria, and every Tuesday she claimed the same armchair near the periodicals, where the newspapers hung from wooden rods like laundry. Today, though, her chair was occupied by Daniel from her civics class, who had spread the city paper, a national paper, and a glossy newsweekly across the table as if he were comparing suspects in a lineup.

"You're in my seat," she said.

"You're in my research." He slid the newsweekly aside without looking up. "Sorry. You can share."

She sat, because the smell of newsprint and old carpet was better than the cafeteria's fryer grease anyway, and because Daniel was tracing something with his pencil. He had drawn arrows from a story about a proposed warehouse development to the small print at the bottom of the page, then to another story, then back again. She leaned in. The arrows formed a little archipelago of circled names across three different publications, and every island was connected to the same company.

"What are you doing?"

"Homework gone sideways," Daniel said. He tapped the masthead of the city paper. "For Mr. Reyes's class I'm reading this book, Manufacturing Consent, by Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky, 1988. They argued that news gets shaped by five filters. The first one is ownership, like when a big corporation owns the outlet."

"Filters," Kate repeated. She said the word the way you repeat a foreign phrase to see if it fits your mouth.

"That's what they called them."

She remembered, suddenly, being eleven, standing in her grandmother's kitchen while the television muttered about a mine that was closing. Her grandmother, who had worked at the hospital for thirty years, said the station never told you who owned the mine, only that the miners were asking for too much. Kate had not understood then what her grandmother was implying; she had thought the news was like weather, something that simply arrived. Now, in the library's yellow light, she wondered whether she had been listening to forecasts all along, or to someone prognosticating with an interest in rain.

She pulled the city paper toward her and found the warehouse story. The development would pave over a field where the county's last community garden stood, a garden where an indigent veterans' group grew vegetables they couldn't otherwise afford. The story was careful, even kind to the veterans, but it ran on page eleven, below a half-page ad for the developer's shopping complex. She flipped to the national paper's version. Different reporter, different city, same company name in the ownership notice, same quiet placement.

"So the book says there are five of these filters," she said slowly, "and ownership is just the first. Which means there are four more we haven't even looked for."

"Which is exactly my problem." Daniel pushed his notes toward her. "I can see the strings on this one puppet. I can't tell if the whole theater works this way, or if some shows are clean. And the book is from 1988, before half these companies even existed."

Kate read down his notes, then back up, then let her eyes rest on the garden veterans' faces, small and gray in the photograph, holding tomatoes like offerings. She thought of her grandmother again, of the closed mine, of all the things a person could suspect without ever proving. Suspicion alone was a kind of laziness, she decided, but so was trusting the page because it was printed. Between the two there had to be a habit of checking, a way of reading with the ownership notice in view, the way you'd check who was selling you a car.

"We could map it," she said. "You and me. Every story about the warehouse, every outlet that runs it, who owns each one. Not because it proves anything, but because then we'd know what we're actually reading."

Daniel looked up for the first time. Outside, a shelf cart squeaked past, and somewhere a printer exhaled a page. "You'd do that?"

"I have until June." She uncapped her pen. "Start with who owns the newsweekly."

Daniel flipped to the front of the glossy magazine, ran his finger along the fine print, and stopped.

"Oh," he said quietly. "Same company as the developer."

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
story:
The math club met on Thursdays in Room 114, the one with the riparian view, its windows overlooking the creek that ran behind the faculty parking lot, and Grayson had claimed the desk by the sill because the light there was good for reading his notebook. He was the youngest member who had stayed after the seniors graduated, and lately he had been working alone on a problem sheet left over from the regional competition, which was this Saturday, three days away. The sheet's last question asked for the area under the curve y equals x squared between zero and three, and beside the word "area" someone had penciled a small arrow pointing to the margin, where the word "integral" waited like a taunt.

He had never computed an integral. He knew the word, knew it belonged to calculus, knew that calculus was a country he was not supposed to enter until college. Priya, a sophomore who sat across from him, kept glancing at his sheet.

"You're doing it the long way," she said. "There's a formula for that."

"I don't know the formula," Grayson said. "I know the picture, though." He drew the curve, then shaded the region beneath it with the side of his pencil. "I want this number."

Priya came around the table and studied his drawing. Her brother was a freshman at the state university, and she had a habit of carrying home phrases from his phone calls. "He talks about Riemann sums," she offered. "For area. That's the only word I remember."

That evening, after dinner, Grayson opened his mother's laptop at the kitchen table and built a spreadsheet. He divided the interval from zero to three into ten equal slices, treated each slice as a thin rectangle whose height matched the curve, multiplied width by height for each one, and summed the results. The total came out below what the shaded picture seemed to promise, because every rectangle left a curved sliver uncounted above it. So he tried again with a hundred rectangles, and the slivers shrank; then a thousand, and the total settled toward a fixed value, changing less with each doubling, like a coin coming to rest. Whatever the true area was, it lay just beyond the number on his screen, and the thinner the rectangles became, the closer the sum pressed against it.

He sat there and let himself cogitate. There were, he decided, two ways to hold the problem. One was the spreadsheet's way, practical and finite: enough rectangles gave an answer good to any tolerance you liked, and Saturday's competition only needed three decimal places. The other was something quieter, an idea he could feel the shape of without naming it: what happened to the sum as the rectangles became infinitely thin. He did not know how mathematicians made "infinitely thin" precise, and he refused to pretend he did. But he wrote both columns in his notebook, the approximate and the imagined, and drew a bracket around them, because he suspected they were the same thing seen from two banks of the same creek.

At Thursday's meeting he showed the notebook to Priya and to Marcus, a junior who had taken the competition twice. "Twenty rectangles gives me this," Grayson said, pointing. "Two hundred gives me this. The numbers keep tightening around something."

Marcus leaned in. "That's a Riemann sum," he said. "That's what it's called."

"And it never actually gets there," Grayson said. "Each one is an approximation. The rectangles get thinner forever." He tapped the bracket. "I think the area is where they're headed. I can't prove it. I can only watch it happen."

Marcus had been the club's formula man, the one who memorized identities and recited them like provenance documents for an antique, each theorem certified by author and date. He had spent ten minutes earlier explaining that competition problems were solved by knowing the right rule. Now he turned the notebook toward himself, copied Grayson's spreadsheet formula onto his own sheet, and entered a hundred thousand in the rectangle column. The restaurant had pushed four tables together in the back room, and the noise of Mathis's graduating class filled it the way water fills a glass, finding every corner. His mother had booked Trattoria Rossi months ago, back when the year still presaged something orderly, and now forty-some people in caps and gowns pushed caps and gowns were actually in the kitchen, clogging a chair, and everyone was eating bread with their hands like children. Mathis sat near the middle, his diploma tube on the tablecloth like a fat crayon, and tried to locate himself inside the celebration.

His cousin Elodie, who had driven three hours and was working on her second glass of prosecco, stood up and clinked a fork against a glass. She gave a short, warm speech about Mathis being the first in their family to finish high school in America, and then, because she was a teacher and could not help herself, she turned to the room. "Look around," she said. "In our school in the ninth grade there were over three hundred of you."

Dario, two seats down, started naming names on his fingers, the way people do at funerals, involuntary andavenous for completeness. "Marcus, who moved. Ana, who had the baby. Terrell, who just stopped coming in March of sophomore year." He got to six names and slowed, frowning, working backward through yearbook memories. Nobody had asked him to do it. The table quieted around him the way a room quiets when someone drops a glass but the glass doesn't break.

"That's like a tenth of them," said Priya, who was cerebral in the way of someone who counted everything twice. "Maybe more. A tenth, an eighth, I don't know."

Mathis had actually looked this up, two weeks ago, at one in the morning, avoiding his history final. "It's not just our school," he said. "The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." The phrase came out of him flat and memorized, and Priya looked at him with something like respect, and Elodie nodded as if he had passed a test she hadn't announced.

"Thirteen percent," said Dario. "That's, what, in our class, of the three hundred and twelve who started ninth grade with us..." He did the arithmetic on a napkin with the restaurant's stubby pencil, tongue between his teeth, and arrived at roughly forty people, and then he looked around the back room as if expecting the forty to materialize, standing wetly by the coat rack. "Forty people," he said again, quieter.

Across the table, Dev was not eating. Dev had started ninth grade with them and had not finished, and he was here anyway because Mathis had texted him three times and then gone to his apartment and stood in the doorway until Dev agreed. Dev's want was simple and enormous: he wanted back in. He had a job at a warehouse and a plan to test for his equivalency diploma in the fall, and what he wanted from tonight, though he would never have said it this way, was verisimilitude, the feeling of still belonging to the class of people in this room, eating bread, arguing about numbers that had names and didn't.

"Congratulations," Dev said to Mathis, and it came out almost angry, and then he seemed to hear it himself and put down the bread he hadn't bitten. "Sorry. I mean it, I do."

Mathis thought about the number, thirteen out of every hundred, and about how he had always understood it as a statistic about other people, a national fact that lived in news articles, and how it was also a napkin in front of Dario with forty names that nobody had actually written down. Both things were true at once and he could not make them into one thing. He slid his diploma tube across the tablecloth to Dev. "Open it," he said.

"You'll smudge it."

"I'm not going to frame it, Dev. Open it."

Dev unscrewed the cap and slid the diploma out, holding it by the edges with his warehouse hands, and read Mathis's name in the embossed script, and then his own lips moved without sound, trying out how the same sentence would look with a different name in it, some other school's seal at the bottom. Priya, who could not stand an unfinished count, pulled the napkin toward herself and began listing the six names Dario had said, writing each one down. "Forty is a made-up number," she said, pencil moving. "These six are real. We start with these." Dev set the diploma down, careful, and leaned over to see the napkin, and asked how she spelled Ana's last name, because he remembered it differently.

Samuel had spent three weeks getting the motion passed, so when the cafeteria went trayless on Monday, he stood by the milk cooler with his clipboard and felt the morning arrange itself around him like a promise. The logic had seemed airtight at the council table: students took less when they had to carry everything by hand, schools that removed trays reported less plate waste, and their own audit, forty pounds of food scraped into bins on an ordinary Tuesday, had embarrassed everyone. He counted the first twenty students through the line. Twelve of them made a second trip.

By Wednesday the second trips had become a habit, and the habit had a shape. Kids grabbed a burger, ate it standing, then returned for fries, then for a cookie, and what they could not finish they abandoned on tables because carrying a half-eaten pastry back to a bin while balancing a drink was apparently a hardship. The custodian, Mr. Reyes, wheeled his gray bin past Samuel at the end of lunch and stopped. "Forty-six pounds today," he said. "I weighed it because I figured you'd want to know, or you'd want not to know. Which is it?" Samuel watched a girl leave a whole apple beside the napkin dispenser, unbruised, and had no answer for him.

The emergency council meeting was held in Mrs. Okafor's room, because Mrs. Okafor had the only open period and had signed the faculty approval form in the first place. She did not rescue them. She sat by the window with her coffee and let Priya defend the plan, let Marcus blame the freshman class, let the treasurer point out that the composting company had already been contracted. Then she asked one question. "Why didn't any of you see it coming?" Nobody spoke. The radiator ticked. Samuel, who had proposed the whole thing, felt the question settle somewhere under his ribs, less an accusation than an assignment.

He went to the public library that night because the school library closed at four and because he did not want anyone watching him research his own failure. In the sociology section, between thick books with cracked spines, he found the essay, and the name attached to it, Robert K. Merton, a sociologist, in a 1936 piece called "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action." He read it at a carrel under a green lamp while a man two seats over titrated, drop by careful drop, cream into his coffee with the concentration of a chemist, and Samuel thought that Merton had done the same thing to human plans, adding case after case until the mixture changed color.

"It's called the unanticipated consequences of purposive social action," Samuel told Priya the next morning, the photocopies flat on the lab bench between them. "That's actually the title." She frowned at the pages. "He lists why it happens," Samuel went on. "Ignorance. Plain error. And here's the one that stings, he says people focus on immediate interests instead of long-term ones." Priya read the last page twice. "We wanted the win by Friday," she said quietly. "The assembly, the announcement, the photo for the paper." Samuel nodded, because that was exactly it, and because nodding was easier than saying aloud that he had wanted his father to see the photo.

They built the fix over two days of skipped free periods. Second trips were fine, Priya argued, if the first trip was free and the second cost less, so no one grabbed extra defensively; Marcus added small trays, half-size, that the dish machine could handle; the treasurer, wincing, found the money by cutting the banner for spirit week. Samuel stood at the milk cooler again on Friday with his clipboard and watched Mr. Reyes weigh the bins. Thirty-one pounds. Better than forty-six, still worse than the forty they had started with, and nobody at the table that afternoon pretended otherwise. The gain had cost them the spirit week banner, the goodwill of the freshman class, and, if Samuel was honest, the clean pleasure of having been right.

The twist came at the end of the day, when Mrs. Okafor called him into the hallway. "You should know something," she said. "The principal's office asked me to sign that approval back in September. They wanted the tray savings on the dish machine for the budget. Your motion was convenient." She held his gaze. "I let it be convenient." Samuel walked out to the bus loop with the photocopies still folded in his jacket, understanding that he had been, in some autochthonous and unflattering way, part of the furniture of a decision that was never entirely his, and that Merton had not covered this part, the part where consequences were intended by someone else all along.

He found Mr. Reyes locking the kitchen door. "So is it fixed?" Mr. Reyes asked, nodding at the clipboard under Samuel's arm. "Some of it," Samuel said. "We're keeping the numbers." Mr. Reyes considered him, an epicure of long shifts evaluating a modest meal, and then held up the scale. "Then come Monday," he said, "you weigh it yourself."
