Jack had one goal for third period: survive his presentation on the sources for the bombing of Hiroshima, and, if the fates allowed, beat Mara Delgado at the argument they'd been having since September. Mara read everything, cited everything, and delivered her corrections in a flat, sardonic voice that made the whole class laugh at whoever she was correcting. Usually Jack. He had spent two weekends in the library and one awkward Sunday at his grandfather's house, and now his backpack held a weapon he hadn't told anyone about.

Mr. Rowley's classroom smelled like chalk dust and radiator heat. The posters were the usual ones, Washington crossing his river, the MLK quote about arcs bending. "Today we're looking at how we know what we know," Mr. Rowley said, and sat on the front desk with his arms folded, which meant he planned to say almost nothing for fifty minutes. Jack went first, and it went badly, quickly. His sources were all from the same side, and Mara said so before he'd even finished, in the flat voice: "All Allied documents. All postwar. That's not evidence, that's an echo."

Jack unzipped the backpack. "Then try this." He set the book on the document camera, and a photograph bloomed on the whiteboard: a textbook cover, gray-green, corner softened by sixty years of hands. It was his grandfather's American history text, kept in a box in the garage. The class leaned in the way people lean toward anything that has survived longer than they have. "Published 1954," Jack said. "Same war. Watch what it says."

He read the paragraph aloud. It took four sentences to explain the decision to use the bomb, and every sentence assumed the decision had been necessary, humane, and closed. There were no Japanese voices in it. There were no questions. It ended by calling the bombing "the final act of a war America had not chosen," and Jack looked up and saw that even Mara had stopped writing.

"That can't be right," said Devon from the back. "That's the same thing our book covers." Their own textbook devoted nine pages, and the second page began with a photograph of a Japanese schoolyard and a question, printed in bold: "What did civilians know, and when?" Jack hadn't picked the old book to make this point. He'd picked it because it was the only primary thing he could get his hands on, and it had seemed, at the time, like happenstance that it disagreed so completely with the book in front of him. Now he stood there feeling the ground shift, because if two textbooks could disagree this much, one of them had to be wrong, and he had no way to tell which, and neither, he suspected, did anyone else in the room.

"My grandma has one like that," Mara said, and her voice wasn't flat anymore. "From her school in the sixties. It tells the whole Vietnam chapter differently. I found it when we were cleaning out her apartment. She got upset when she saw me reading it, so I put it back." She paused. "I keep thinking about which one she believed when she was our age, and whether she ever got told there was another version."

Mr. Rowley uncrossed his arms. "There's a word for what you two have stumbled onto," he said, and then, because he was the kind of teacher who refused to lecture, he wrote it on the board instead: historiography. "The study of how history has been written. Interpretations of the same events, changing over time." He capped the marker. "Jack, why don't you tell us what your two books disagree about. Not conclusions. Underlying things."

Jack looked at the projected page and tried to slow himself down, because he could feel the class waiting and he did not want to guess wrong in front of Mara again. "The old book doesn't ask who the sources left out," he said finally. "Ours asks that on every page. But that's not the same as ours being true. Ours might be asking better questions with still-partial evidence. The people in 1954 weren't lying. They had what they had, and they wrote from where they stood." He heard himself interpolate between the two books, filling the gap with something he couldn't fully verify, a middle account that was fairer than either and proven by neither, and he said so. "I can't tell you which version is right. I can tell you why they differ."

"So nothing's true?" Devon asked, disgusted, the way people always asked that question, as if it were a trap.

"That's not what he said," Mara said, and Jack turned to look at her, because for the first time in four years she wasn't correcting him. "He said the sources are partial and the questions keep changing. That's different."

The bell was two minutes away and nobody moved. Mr. Rowley asked, quietly, whether anyone wanted to bring in other old textbooks for a comparison wall, and five hands went up, including Mara's, and Jack realized he was still standing in front of the class holding his grandfather's book, and that he very much wanted to read the one in her grandmother's apartment. When the bell rang, Mara stopped at his desk on her way out.

"My grandma's on Sundays," she said. "Bring the book."

Tristan had claimed the carrel by the window on the second floor of the county library every Tuesday for six weeks, and he had the tracker open on his laptop again: S.214, a bill to let seventeen-year-olds preregister to vote so that the franchise would reach them automatically on their eighteenth birthdays. He had found it as a draft someone had posted online, watched it get assigned to committee, watched the committee mark it up until an amendment he hated had been stripped out, and then followed the floor debate, which a C-SPAN archive let him replay at one in the morning. The House had passed it. The Senate had passed it, minus the amendment, which meant both chambers had to vote on the same text again, and they had. Then the bill went to the president, and the tracker's status line had sat there, yellow, reading "presented," for what felt like forever.

"They still haven't signed it," Tristan said to Priya, who had the next carrel over and was ostensibly studying for the MCAT. "Eleven days now. It's dead, right? If he doesn't sign, doesn't it just die?"

Priya looked up from a flashcard about the renal system. "Why are you asking me? I know kidneys."

"You enfranchise an entire cohort of people one year early on paper and then the paper just sits there. It's infuriating." He turned the laptop toward her. "Look. Everything happened. Drafting, committee, both votes, everything, and now nothing."

Priya set down the flashcard with the particular care of someone buying time. Her own want that semester was simpler and somehow harder: a summer research position in a lab in Toronto, cosmopolitan and far from this town, and the application required a personal statement she had rewritten eleven times because she could not decide whether honesty or polish was the better artifice. "Have you actually looked up the rule," she said, "or are you just staring at the yellow box?"

He had been just staring at the yellow box. He typed. The reference desk had a copy of the Constitution in paperback, but he didn't need it; the answer was in a Senate glossary page, and he read it twice, then a third time, because it seemed to contradict the yellow box. "Priya. If the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, and Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature."

"That's a sentence," Priya agreed.

"No, it's a loophole. It's the system working. It's the system working in a way nobody tells you about." He counted on his fingers, muttering, "Ten days, Sundays excepted, Congress in session." Eleven calendar days with two Sundays in them came to nine counting days. The yellow box wasn't dead. The yellow box was early. He felt slightly dizzy, the way he had when a physics teacher once showed him that the centrifugal force he'd argued about for a semester wasn't a force at all.

He called the office of his congresswoman, whose aide had answered his email about the bill a month before with a form letter so bland it had to be artifice. A different aide picked up, younger, clearly an intern. Tristan explained who he was and asked, as calmly as he could, whether the count of days excluded Sundays.

"Sundays excepted," the intern said. "Yeah. We had a whole training on it."

"And it's law even if he never signs it."

"Pocket veto's the other thing," the intern said, "that's if Congress is out. Congress is in. So it just becomes law. Honestly it happens more than people think. Was there anything else? I'm supposed to be sorting mail."

Tristan hung up and sat very still. He had spent six weeks believing that the process was a machine for killing things, that the yellow box was the system's way of shrugging. Now he understood that the silence itself could be a kind of assent, and that the machinery had more gears than the diagram in his civics textbook, and he didn't know yet whether that made him more hopeful or less. Both felt true. He decided he was allowed to hold both.

The tracker updated at 4:32 the next afternoon, while Priya was reading her personal statement aloud to the empty carrel to hear where it rang false. "Priya," Tristan said. "S.214. Law. Without a signature."

She stopped mid-sentence, looked over, and grinned at him, the first unguarded grin he'd seen from her in weeks. "You realize you now know more about this than the president apparently did." She tapped her statement on the desk. "Listen to this part, tell me if it sounds like me. And then we're going downstairs to the vending machine, because if a bill can become law by sitting quietly for ten days, Sundays excepted, I can survive one more draft."

story:
The flyer had been taped to the lamppost outside the corner store since August, and Abigail had walked past it every morning without reading it, the way you walk past anything that has decided to be part of the sidewalk. FAST CASH, it said. NO CREDIT CHECK. She read it properly for the first time on a Tuesday in October, because Marisol was standing in front of it with her phone in her hand, thumb hovering, not moving.

"I'm two hundred short on rent," Marisol said. "My mom gets paid Friday, but rent's due Thursday. The landlord already stuck a notice on the door once."

"So ask her for it early."

"She doesn't have it early. That's the whole point of a paycheck." Marisol tapped the number on the flyer. "Fifteen per hundred. That's not bad, right? Thirty bucks to not get evicted."

Abigail did the arithmetic in her head, then did it again because the first answer annoyed her. Fifteen per hundred, for two weeks. Two weeks was one twenty-sixth of a year. Thirty dollars on two hundred, stretched across a year, was thirty multiplied twenty-six times. She said the number out loud before she fully believed it. "That's almost four hundred percent a year."

Marisol laughed, one short syllable. "Nobody keeps it for a year."

"Okay, but still." Abigail took out her own phone and searched, and there it was on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's site, plain as a bus schedule: a typical payday loan fee of fifteen dollars per hundred borrowed, for two weeks, works out to an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent. APR, the page called it, as if naming it made it friendlier.

They were late for first period by then, and Mr. Okafor made his usual remark about the bell being a hermeneutic text that certain students refused to interpret. Nobody laughed, including him. In third period, Abigail sat with her graphing calculator under the desk and ran the other direction, the one nobody put on flyers. Her grandmother had started a certificate of deposit for her when she was nine, three hundred dollars, and every statement showed the balance creeping upward, the interest earning its own interest, small and patient and going the right way. She wrote both numbers in the margin of her chemistry notes: 312.40 and 336.09, the balance now and the projected balance at twenty-two. Money sitting still and growing. Money borrowed and swelling. The same principle, pointed opposite ways, and she thought of a river that could flow in whichever direction you dug.

At lunch Marisol had already half decided. "It's one time," she said, tearing the crust off her sandwich. "I pay it back Friday and it's done."

"Except Friday you're thirty dollars poorer than you already were, and next month the same thing happens."

"You want to litigate my whole life over a loan?"

"No." Abigail pushed her tray an inch away. "I want you to do one math problem before you sign anything."

"I did the math. Thirty bucks."

"That's the fee. That's not the math." She turned the calculator toward Marisol, the screen showing 390, which she'd multiplied out on the assumption of a year, knowing full well Marisol would never hold the loan that long and feeling slightly dishonest about it, the way a frightening statistic always felt a little dishonest even when it was true. "Almost four hundred percent APR. That's what the government's own consumer bureau says it is. That's the real price of the money."

Marisol looked at the screen for a long moment. Down the table, some juniors were arguing about the volleyball roster, and the cafeteria smelled like steam and disinfectant, and Abigail had a sudden atavistic memory of being seven and watching her mother count bills at the kitchen table, whisper-numbering them, and she understood that Marisol was somewhere in that kitchen too, that they both were, and that this was why the flyer worked.

"My aunt could lend it," Marisol said finally, not looking up. "She'll make a face about it, but."

"Faces are cheaper."

Marisol snapped her phone shut and stood, and Abigail watched her walk toward the trash line with the flyer still crumpled in her fist, watched her hold it over the bin, and then, at the last second, smooth it out and put it in her back pocket instead.

story:
Oliver had claimed the corner table by the periodicals an hour before opening on Saturdays was even a thing he did, and now it was a thing he did. Around him the library filled with the small sounds of other people's seriousness: a page turning, a chair scraped back, the printer coughing somewhere behind biography. He had eleven books, four of them useful, and a deadline in nine days for the first real research paper of his life, the kind with an argument instead of a summary, footnotes instead of vibes. His thesis, scrawled on a napkin and then recopied onto the first page of his notebook, was that cities should not have demolished their streetcar lines in the mid-century, and that the case for doing so had rested less on evidence than on fashion. He liked the thesis. He did not yet know how to prove it.

The proving was the trouble. His history teacher had handed out a sheet titled "Chicago, MLA, or APA: Pick One and Be Consistent," and Oliver had picked Chicago because the sample page looked the most like something a person with a pipe would write. But the sheet assumed vocabulary he did not have. Bibliography. Annotated. Citation style. He had footnoted things before, sort of, in the loose way you footnote when you're afraid of being accused of stealing. He understood that ideas had owners. He had not understood that ideas had filing systems.

Priya arrived at ten with a coffee the size of a fire hydrant and dropped into the chair across from him. She was technically his writing club partner, which meant they met Thursdays in Mr. Okafor's room, but Saturdays at the library had become their own arrangement, unspoken, unaudited. She was working on a paper about the Arthur Miller hearings, which Oliver suspected was a better topic than streetcars, though he would not have said so. She leaned over his sprawl of note cards and read the napkin transcription upside down, a skill she had and he envied.

"You have an argument," she said. "That's the hard part. Mostly done."

"Mostly not done. I have to cite everything. There are rules about the order."

"There are." She flipped to his draft bibliography, a page he'd assembled the night before by listing sources in the order he'd happened to use them, the encyclopedia first because he'd started there, then the transit history, then the planning commission report he'd found at eleven at night. She tapped it. "This is in the wrong order. In Chicago, MLA and APA, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited."

Oliver looked at the page as if she'd told him it was upside down. "That seems backwards."

"It seems like a library." She shrugged, laconic about it, as though she had not just relocated his entire evening. "Think of it as a catalog. You don't shelve books by when someone last pulled them off the shelf."

He spent forty minutes reordering the page, and it was during the reordering that the trouble started. The transit history and a journal article he'd found through the library's database disagreed, sharply, about whether ridership had already been collapsing before the demolitions. He had cited both, one after the other, comfortable in their sequence, and now, forced to alphabetize them apart from each other, he could see the seam. Smethers said collapse. Volkening said sabotage, meaning the companies had run down service on purpose and then pointed at the ruins as evidence. Alphabetical order had not created the disagreement. It had only refused to let him hide it.

He sat with that for a while, chin on his fist, watching a man two tables over adjudicate something loudly with a librarian over a hold notice. At home, his father, who drove a bus for a living and had opinions about streetcars that began and ended with the word "obsolete," had already delivered his verdict on the paper over dinner. "You want culpability," his father had said, pointing a fork at him. "Somebody to blame. Write it so it's somebody's fault, and you'll get your A." Oliver had not answered, because the honest answer was that he didn't know yet whether it was somebody's fault, and saying so at the table would have started a thing.

That night he wrote to his grandfather, his mother's father, who had ridden the streetcars as a boy and who answered letters because he had never quite taken to the phone. Oliver asked him point-blank whether the cars had been dying when they went. He sealed the envelope before he could soften the question.

The reply came Thursday, in the narrow looping hand his grandfather had retained from a school system Oliver couldn't picture. "They were dying the way a neglected animal dies," the letter said. "Whether that counts as dying, you will have to decide, but do not let the men who neglected it tell you what dying looks like." Then a paragraph about a conductor named Havel who let boys ride free in rain, and a postscript: "Your mother says you are going to college. Good. Learn to distrust whoever wrote the summary."

On Saturday Oliver spread the letter beside the note cards and the reordered bibliography, Smethers under S, Volkening under V, the encyclopedia filed under its corporate name like a person with no first name. He read the two clashing passages again. His thesis still stood, but it had grown a hinge, a place where it could open onto something less satisfying: that the case against the streetcars had been an argument about evidence made by people who had arranged the evidence. He drafted a footnote that gave both sources, then a sentence in the body that gave neither of them full custody of the truth.

Priya read the paragraph over his shoulder while he pretended not to notice. "So which one is right?" she said.

"I don't know yet," Oliver said, and pulled the page back toward him, and wrote it anyway.

story:
The paycheque lay on the break-room table at Halloran's Hardware for a full minute before David picked it up. He had been saving since June, and this was the first cheque with real hours on it, forty of them, two weeks of stocking shelves and hauling fertilizer bags. At the top, under gross pay, the numbers began subtracting themselves: federal income tax, Ontario income tax, something called CPP, something called EI. He did the subtraction twice on the back of a paint sample card and arrived at the same smaller number both times.

"You're staring at it like it insulted you," said Rosie, who ran the register and had worked at Halloran's since before the store expanded into the garden centre.

"Fourteen percent of it is just gone," David said. "Before I even see it."

"That's not gone, that's CPP, that's your pension someday, and EI is if you get laid off." She tapped the two income tax lines. "Those come back around in April if they took too much. You file a return, you claim deductions, tuition counts." She was already walking back toward the front, calling over her shoulder, "Ask your dad."

His father was the problem, though. In March, before any of this, David had watched him spread receipts across the kitchen table for three nights running, muttering about mileage and moving expenses, before sealing the return in an envelope with the grim finality of a man posting an indictment. When David had asked what a deduction actually was, his father had said, "Money you spent to make money, so they tax you on less of it," and then, quieter, "I'm not the person to ask. I always feel like I'm getting away with something, and I never am." That was the flashback he kept returning to, his father's hands flat on the table, the envelope, the door closing behind it.

That afternoon a customer came in wanting a refund for a wet-vac that had leaked across her basement floor, and the manager, Mr. Halloran, told her the manufacturer's warranty was her indemnity, not the store, though he would process the return as a courtesy. David rang it through while she lectured him about impermeable seals and how the advertising had promised an impermeable tank, whatever the box said. She left with her refund and he stood there holding the receipt she had refused, and on it, below the subtotal, was a single line: HST 13%.

He had been in Toronto the previous weekend with Priya, and at the restaurant she had squinted at their bill and said, "Where's the GST? And the Ontario tax? They only charged us one thing." The server, passing with a tray, had said, "Harmonized Sales Tax, one line, thirteen percent," and kept walking, and Priya had shrugged and Venmoed her half. David had pocketed the bill because he was saving receipts now, because that was the plan: keep everything, learn the system his father flinched from, walk into his first return next April knowing more than the man across the table had ever wanted to.

So after close, he sat in the break room with the rejected wet-vac receipt, his own paycheque stub, and the restaurant bill, arranging them like evidence. The cheque showed what the government took before he was paid. The receipts showed what was added when he spent, one line, thirteen percent, the same in Toronto as here. He understood, in a preliminary way, that the two systems touched each other somewhere, that the deductions his father hunted were the hinge between them, and he understood equally that he did not yet understand the hinge. He texted Priya: "Is your uncle still an accountant?" She replied with a thumbs up and "He owes me for math tutoring."

On Saturday he bought a notebook with a cover the colour of a school bus and wrote Sept 12 on the first page. He pasted nothing in yet. He copied the lines from the paycheque stub into columns, then the HST line from the restaurant bill, then a question mark where the connection should be. Priya's uncle had agreed to coffee on the twenty-third, which David had written in pen, which felt like a commitment he was not entirely prepared for. He did not know whether he would file his own return in April or end up at the kitchen table with his father, two envelopes, the same dread. Both futures seemed available to him, and he could not yet tell which one he was choosing, or whether choosing was even how it worked.

Mr. Halloran knocked on the break-room frame. "Lock up when you're done conspiring," he said, and handed David the store's copy of the wet-vac refund slip. "File that somewhere sensible. People who keep their paper sleep better."

David put it in the notebook, between the columns and the question mark, and closed the cover.

story:
The clay was too dry by the time Leah got home, and she knew it before she touched it. The bag had sat open on the porch rail since morning, and the August heat had taken what the plastic was supposed to hold in. She worked it anyway, pressing her thumb into a ball that cracked at the edges like old paint, and decided she would wedge in water slowly, the way Dara had shown her at the studio, patient as kneading bread.

She was making a set of cups for her grandmother, who had given up her own studio three winters ago when her hands began shaking. The design was simple, five cups with a carved line spiraling from rim to base, but the clay was not the kind she had learned on. Her grandmother had left behind a shelf of materials, half-labeled, and Leah had chosen a white bag with no writing on it at all because it felt smooth, almost creamy, between her fingers.

At the studio on Tuesday she brought a test piece to fire, a small pinch bowl that had come out of her practice session better than she expected. Marcus, who ran the kilns on Thursdays, weighed the bowl in one hand and frowned.

"What clay is this?" he asked, and when she shrugged he set it apart from the row of earthenware waiting on the shelf. "Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius," he said. "Porcelain has to go between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius. It can't ride along with the rest."

Leah stared at the little bowl, suddenly aware that she had almost ruined a whole kiln load, or at least her own work, by guessing. She had assumed firing was firing, one heat for everything, the way she had assumed a year ago that her grandmother's silence about the studio meant she didn't want to talk about it at all.

She thought about that silence now, wedging the reclaimed clay at the kitchen table while the radio muttered in the corner. Her grandmother had stopped answering questions about glazes, about the wood kiln she had built with two other potters in 1988, and Leah had taken the refusal as a door closing rather than a door that was heavy. It was Dara, finally, who had set her straight, though not in words. Dara had simply kept showing up at the old woman's apartment with her obstreperous little terrier and her half-finished mugs, until one afternoon the three of them were at the table and Leah's grandmother picked up a mug, turned it over, and said the handle was set too low for a hand that knew what it was doing. It was the closest thing to praise she had given anyone in two years.

There was a letter in Leah's desk drawer that she had started and abandoned in June, before any of this. She got it out now and read it under the kitchen lamp.

"Dear Grandma," it began, in her careful cursive, "I'm sorry I didn't visit more this spring. I kept thinking you wanted the quiet, and it was easier to believe that than to drive over and find out. I've started going to the community studio on Cutter Street. Dara comes too. Last week my bowl cracked in the kiln because I rushed the drying, and instead of quitting I made another one, which I think you would appreciate, though you'd never say so. I'm trying to decide whether the cups should be porcelain or the brown earthenware. If you want to tell me what you'd do, I'll listen. If you don't, I'll figure it out myself, and I'll still bring them when they're done."

She had never sent it. It sat in the drawer like a second self, braver and more honest, and Leah had told herself she was waiting for the cups to be finished first, as if the letter needed a gift attached to be deliverable. Tonight she read it and understood that this was a lie, though a small one, the kind a person acclimates to until it stops feeling like a lie at all. She folded the paper, opened her phone, and photographed the letter instead. Then she sent the image to her grandmother with a single line beneath it: I wrote this in June. It's still true, except now I know the white clay is porcelain, so it has to go in the hotter load, and I'm glad.

The reply came while she was still pressing the spiral lines into the third cup, her fingertips ridge after ridge down the curve of the wall. Her grandmother had typed, slowly and with visible effort, "Porcelain wants 1,200 to 1,400. Your grandfather always fired it too cool because he was impatient. Don't be impatient. And don't use my old glaze book, the recipes are wrong on page nine."

Leah laughed out loud in the empty kitchen, a short sound that surprised her. She set the phone face-up on the table where she could see it, squared her shoulders over the fourth cup, and began to carve the line that spiraled down toward the base, steady, unhurried, all the way around.

story:
Connor's father folded himself into the passenger seat with the caution of a man entering a canoe, adjusted the mirror twice, and said, "Six days until the test. Let's not waste tonight."

The car was a spartan old sedan, manual locks, no backup camera, a radio that only picked up one station out here at the edge of the suburbs. Connor had been reading the driver's manual all week, but reading was one genus of knowledge and driving, he was discovering, was another entirely. The engine started on the second try. He let the parking brake down too fast and the car lurched, and his father's hand went to the dash, though he said nothing, which was somehow worse.

They rolled down Sycamore, a street so quiet that the sprinklers seemed loud. Connor kept drifting toward the curb and correcting, drifting and correcting, a stitching motion his father finally interrupted. "You're aiming at the hood ornament. Look far ahead, where you want to go." It helped, which annoyed him, because Dev had told him the same thing two days ago at lunch, along with advice Connor had liked better: "Following distance, two seconds, that's all you need. Three is for grandmas. You leave three and everybody cuts in."

Dev had his license already, had failed once and passed the second time, and had lambasted the examiner on principle regardless. Connor had believed him, mostly because Dev said everything with total certainty and because two seconds felt like the kind of efficient, adult thing a person with places to be would do. His father, when the subject came up at the end of Sycamore, waiting to turn onto the busier avenue, said only, "National Safety Council says at least three seconds." Not a lecture, not a speech. Just the sentence, delivered while checking the intersection.

"Dev says two," Connor said, and turned. A delivery van appeared in his mirror, closer than he expected, and his stomach dropped a little.

"Dev drives a car his dad bought him with a bow on it," his father said. "Three. And you count it off a fixed object, a sign, a driveway. Watch."

They practiced it. A speed limit sign slid past and his father said "now," and Connor counted one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two, one-thousand-three, and the driveway they'd chosen arrived at the count of three, roughly. His father made him do it again at a mailbox, then again at a fire hydrant, until the counting became rhythm instead of arithmetic. Then the light ahead turned yellow and the sky, which had been merely gray since four o'clock, opened up into a thin, steady rain, and the wipers scraped across a dry streak on the left side.

"Rain's a difficulty," his father said. "You add a second for each difficulty. So now what?"

Connor looked at the van ahead, at the wet sheen on the asphalt, at the brake lights blooming red and smeary through the windshield. He wanted to say that Dev would keep it at two and gun the yellow. Instead he counted to four off a manhole cover, and when traffic slowed suddenly for someone turning left, he had the space to ease off the gas instead of standing on the brake. The car behind him honked anyway, and his father said, "Let them. They're not taking your test."

They drove the loop twice more, through the rain and then out the far side of it, where the pavement was dry again and the evening light came low and orange between the houses. Connor found that he could hold three seconds now without counting out loud, that it had become something he could feel in the distance, the way he could feel the clutch point in his foot. He thought about Dev saying two, and his father saying three, and the van behind him riding his bumper as though distance were a personal insult. It occurred to him that the rule wasn't really about seconds; the seconds were just a way of pricing what the road was costing you today, rain, traffic, dusk, each one added up. He still wasn't sure where Dev's confidence came from or whether he'd ever have it, or even whether he wanted it. Two seconds was faster. Three was a bet that the world would surprise you, and tonight, at least, the world had obliged.

Back in the driveway, engine off, his father pulled the key and pocketed it before Connor could ask for another lap. "Six days," he said. "Same time tomorrow."

"Can we do the avenue again?" Connor asked. "In the rain, if it rains."

His father looked at him for a moment, then unlocked the door to get out. "Bring a jacket," he said.

story:
The draft came back on a Thursday with a red margin note that read, in Mr. Okoye's cramped hand: "This is a fact, not a thesis. What are you actually arguing?" Ashton had written nine pages on the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, and his opening sentence, underlined twice, stated that the law denied enslaved people legal rights. Mr. Okoye had circled it and written "Everyone accepts this" beside the circle, and then, at the bottom, "Revision due Monday. Footnotes this time. Chicago style."

He had been planning to spend the weekend at his grandfather's house anyway, his mother dropping him off with a duffel bag and a grocery bag of his grandmother's oatmeal cookies, and so he spread the problem across the dining room table on Saturday morning like a surveyor laying out terrain. His grandfather, a retired history professor, put down his coffee and looked at the pages for a long moment without touching them.

"So the man wants footnotes," his grandfather said. "Good. Footnotes are where you show your work. Like a carpenter leaving the joints visible."

"Can you just tell me what to argue?" Ashton asked.

"No." His grandfather picked up his mug and carried it toward the sunroom, where the light was better for the crossword. "But there's a box of my old handbooks in the closet if you want company. Don't disturb the mice."

The box held forty years of style guides, some older than Ashton's mother. He found the citation format easily enough; Chicago wanted numbered footnotes at the bottom of the page, a full citation the first time, shorter after that, and a bibliography alphabetized at the end. He practiced on the back of a utility bill, writing his own name into a fake citation, and felt a small, private satisfaction at how official it looked. But the thesis problem kept circling back. He went looking for it the way his grandfather had taught him to look for anything, by finding the shelf where an answer might live.

In a handbook from 1974, under a section about forming an argument, he read a sentence he copied onto an index card because it seemed to belong to someone more organized than he was: a research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts. He read it twice. Then he read his own circled sentence again and felt his ears go warm, the way they did when a joke landed a beat after the punchline. His whole draft had been standing on something nobody would ever bother to fight about. It wasn't wrong; it was worse than wrong, in a way, because there was nothing to do with it. A fact just sat there. You couldn't lean on it.

"I found something," he said, carrying the index card to the sunroom.

His grandfather read it over the top of his glasses. "Arguable," he said, and handed the card back. "That's the word your teacher wants."

Ashton sat on the floor beside the crossword chair and started pulling the thread. If a thesis had to be something a reasonable person could dispute, then somewhere out there was a reasonable person who would dispute his, and he had to imagine that person clearly enough to answer them. His grandfather, it turned out, had spent two decades studying dissident writers, Czech and Russian ones, people whose crime had been publishing things that everybody in power agreed were not worth disputing. "They got prison for arguing," his grandfather said, filling in a seven-letter word for patience. "So I've always had a soft spot for a good dispute." Which raised a question Ashton liked better than any he'd started with: who, in 1850, had actually argued that the Fugitive Slave Act was a good thing, and what did they say, and were they stupid or just afraid or something more complicated?

His first new thesis was too big, something about the whole North being complicit, and his grandfather disabused him of it over lunch by asking four questions he could not answer, none of them cruel. His second drifted into territory about the economics of shipping routes, which was interesting but tangential, and Ashton cut it himself before anyone could point that out, noticing as he did that cutting his own favorite paragraph felt like a kind of growing up, though he wouldn't have said so. The third attempt he wrote on the index card and turned face down while he worked on the footnotes, because he wanted to come back to it cold, the way Mr. Okoye would.

By Sunday evening he had eleven pages, twenty-three footnotes, a bibliography with both primary and secondary sources separated the way the handbook showed, and a thesis he thought a reasonable person could genuinely hate: that Northern judges who enforced the law were not simply cowards, but men who believed they were saving the Union, and that this belief did more damage than cowardice would have. He was not sure it was right. He was not even sure he believed it on Tuesdays. But it could be argued with, and that seemed, for the first time all weekend, like a real thing for a paper to be.

His grandfather read the last page standing at the counter, still holding his reading glasses in one hand. "I'd dispute this," he said finally. "I'd dispute it hard."

"Is that bad?"

"It's the point." He set the pages down and squared their edges against the counter with two sharp taps. "Monday, then."

On Monday morning Ashton got to school early and slid the revision under Mr. Okoye's door before first period, and it was only at lunch, checking his citations one more time in the library, that he discovered the entire bibliography was still in his grandfather's kitchen, sitting beside the cookie tin, exactly where he had left it.

Tyson had forty minutes before his grandfather's Buick had to be back in the driveway, because Grandpa had a card game at noon and the car was his ride. That was the whole window: one driving lesson, in the parking lot of the closed Kmart and then on the flat streets behind it, with his grandfather sitting in the passenger seat folding and unfolding the map he refused to use.

"Clutch, no. This is an automatic, boy. Just brake and gas." Grandpa tapped the dashboard with two knuckles. "Now, first thing you learn, and I mean learn it good. If you ever have to stop fast, you pump the brakes. On and off, on and off, or you'll lock up and slide straight into whatever you're heading for. Your father learned it that way. I learned it that way."

Tyson put the key in and turned it, and the engine caught, and something in his chest did too. He had waited all summer for this. In September he would be at college in a town where nobody drove him anywhere, and the difference between a person with a license and a person without had started to feel like the difference between two separate lives. He eased out of the driveway, the whole car feeling borrowed and enormous, and did not mention that the instructor from the driving school, a calm woman named Ms. Okafor, was coming at eleven.

She arrived while Grandpa was still lecturing, and she contextualized the whole arrangement in one sentence: "So you're the experienced driver, I'm the certified one, and Tyson gets both of us." Grandpa laughed at that, maybe harder than the joke deserved, and moved to the back seat with his map.

They did laps of the Kmart lot, and Tyson found the bite of the steering wheel in his hands, the way a turn was a conversation rather than a command. Then Ms. Okafor had him pull to the edge of the lot. "Before we go on the street, one thing. This car has anti-lock brakes. In a real emergency, you press the brake firmly and hold it, all the way down, and you keep holding. Don't pump. And you can still steer while you're braking." She said it once, flat and quick, and moved on to mirror positions, as if it were no more important than anything else.

Grandpa's voice came from the back seat. "That can't be right."

"That's the current training," Ms. Okafor said, not turning around.

Tyson drove them out onto Fenwick Road, and for ten minutes there was only the small work of it, signaling, checking, the reverie of imagining himself pulling into a dorm parking lot next fall broken by Ms. Okafor's hand on the dash. A dog, a big one, cream-colored, had come off a porch and was standing dead center in the road. There was no time to be polite about it.

He pressed the brake, hard, and held it. The pedal did something under his foot, a quick shuddering he had never felt before, and the car slowed with a grinding sound like the whole machine was arguing with itself, and Grandpa shouted "Pump it, pump," from behind, and Tyson held on because holding was the thing he had been told, and the wheel was still alive in his hands, so he steered. The Buick came to a stop angled toward the curb, and the dog, unbothered, trotted around the front bumper and sat down on the lawn it had come from.

Nobody said anything for a moment. Then Grandpa said, quietly, "We would have slid into that fence in my day."

"Your day's brakes were different," Ms. Okafor said, and Tyson felt the two of them settle something without his having to referee it. He had heard both versions now, the pumping and the holding, one from a man who had driven fifty years without an accident and one from a woman with a clipboard, and he could not have said which teaching tradition was wiser overall, only that today, in this car, the new way had stopped them. Maybe the old way had saved other people on ice in 1974. He would probably pump if he ever drove Grandpa's first truck, if that truck still existed anywhere but in stories. Some things stayed uncertain, and he let them.

He signaled, checked the mirror, and pulled back onto Fenwick Road. In the back seat Grandpa folded his antiquated map into a small square and tucked it into his jacket pocket, and Tyson drove home three minutes under the wire, stopping smoothly at every sign.

At the curb, Grandpa leaned forward between the seats. "You held it," he said. "Good instinct."

"It wasn't instinct," Tyson said. "She told me."

Grandpa patted the shoulder of the seat twice, almost like patting Tyson himself. "Same thing, at your age." Then he got out, straightened his jacket, and walked up the driveway whistling toward the house, calling back over his shoulder, "Card game at noon, but the evening's free. Want to drive me there instead?"

story:
Marcus had told everyone at school that his grandfather walked out of a factory in 1985 and never went back, which was true in the sense that he once left early on a Tuesday and true in no other sense. The assignment was an interview about work, due Monday, and Marcus had put it off until the last possible dinner, so now the recorder app on his phone sat between the salt shaker and his grandfather's plate like a small stone nobody wanted to touch.

"Ask him about the union," his mother said, ladling stew. "That's the interesting part." His grandfather made a noise that could have been agreement or the opposite. Marcus pressed record.

"Did you ever go on strike?" Marcus asked. He was imagining picket lines, the way he imagined most things, in movie lighting.

"We voted on one. Never had to walk." His grandfather tore a piece of bread and dragged it through the stew. "We had a contract. Every three years we sat down across from the company and argued about wages, hours, safety. If we couldn't agree, we could strike, and they knew it, so mostly we agreed." He chewed for a while. Marcus found himself leaning forward without deciding to.

"So the union got you your wage?"

"The union got us the table. We brought the wage to it." His grandfather looked at Marcus in that way he had, as if checking whether the boy was worth the trouble of the explanation. "Union members were common then. Ordinary. Your teacher would tell you it's not like that anymore."

That night Marcus looked it up, because the internet made looking things up a kind of reflex, like swallowing. The Bureau of Labor Statistics had a page. Union membership among wage and salary workers was 10.0 percent in 2025. He scrolled and found the older number, from 1983: 20.1 percent. He did the subtraction twice. Roughly half, and then roughly half again, like a photograph fading in stages. He sat with the two numbers longer than the assignment required, wondering what a country looks like when twice as many people bargain together, or when half as many do, and whether it looks like anything at all from the outside.

He texted his friend Dana, who worked weekends at the coffee place by the highway. "Do you get overtime after 40 hours?" he typed. "legally yes," she wrote back, "but they schedule me 39.5 so they never have to pay it. also no breaks some shifts. manager says if I don't like it there's a line of applicants." She added a thumbs up, which he understood to be bitter. He thought about his grandfather's table, the company on one side and everyone on the other, and about Dana alone in a room where the other side held all the chairs. He wrote back, "there's supposed to be a law about breaks," and she wrote, "there is. it's load-bearing the way a screen door is load-bearing," and then, "anyway how's the history paper." It wasn't a history paper, exactly, but he let that stand.

At the next dinner he brought the numbers with him the way you bring a present you're not sure will fit. "I found it," he said. "Ten percent of wage and salary workers are union members now. In 2025. It was 20.1 percent in 1983." He said it carefully, all of it, because he'd promised himself he wouldn't get it wrong in front of his grandfather.

His grandfather set down his fork. "Half," he said. "In my working life, half."

"You said you walked out of the factory," Marcus said, and felt something shift under him.

"I retired from it. Thirty-one years. Dues card in my wallet the whole time." His grandfather took the wallet out, an old leather thing gone soft as cloth, and thumbed through it without finding whatever he was looking for. "You've been telling people the other version?"

"I might have improved it," Marcus admitted. His mother laughed into her water glass. He was aware that he improved things often, that his memory was a painting rather than a photograph, and that this was a problem he hadn't solved and wasn't solving now. He thought about writing the interview up honestly, strike vote and all, and about how much duller it was than the version he'd been carrying around, and how the dull version had a kind of weight the shiny one didn't.

"Write down what I actually said," his grandfather told him. "The table part. The part where nobody walked out because we didn't have to." He pushed his plate toward the center of the table, where the stew bowl sat between them, and tapped the wood twice with two fingers, the way a man knocks on a door he half expects to be answered.

"Pass the bread," he said.

story:
The popcorn machine had a smell Luke could already tell he would stop noticing by August, the way he'd stopped noticing the chlorine smell at the neighborhood pool after two summers of swim lessons. The manager, a woman named Corinna with a lanyard full of keys, walked him past the concession stand toward a cramped office in back where the walls sequestered the noise of the lobby into a muffled hum. She slid a laminated sheet across the desk, and there it was: eight dollars an hour, weekends and two weeknights, a start date circled in green pen.

"You're hired," she said, "pending the paperwork, which is mostly the part where you promise not to steal candy." She said it without smiling, which made it hard to tell whether it was a joke or a test.

The person training him on concessions was a tall, morose senior named Dev who wore his visor like it had been assigned to him as a punishment. Dev showed him how to layer the butter in thirds so it reached the bottom of the bucket, how to tear the ticket stubs with one motion, how to spot the customers who would ask for a refund no matter what you did for them. By the second week Luke had the rhythm of it, and Dev had begun, grudgingly, to talk.

"I'm gone at the end of the month," Dev said one Tuesday while they restocked napkin dispensers. "Maybe sooner. I got a better gig at the climbing gym. I'm thinking I just don't show up. Let her figure it out."

"Wouldn't you give notice? Two weeks or whatever?"

Dev laughed, a single dry note. "Why? What are they going to do, fire me?"

That night Luke sat on his bedroom floor with his phone and looked it up, because Dev's answer had felt too easy, the way things feel easy when someone has already decided. He found it on a state government page, plain as a bus schedule: most employment in the United States is at-will, which means the employer can end the job at any time, for any reason that isn't illegal, and the worker can quit the same way. No notice required on either side. He read it twice. Something about the symmetry unsettled him, though he couldn't have said why at first, and he fell asleep still holding the phone.

The next shift, a Saturday, the lobby smelled like rain because a storm had chased a whole showing's worth of people inside early, dripping and loud. Luke found Dev behind the counter wiping down the pretzel warmer with the commitment of someone performing a small funeral. Luke had spent the walk over assembling what he thought of as his case, a little structure of reasons, though he was aware that stacking reasons was not the same as being right.

"You don't have to give notice," Luke said. "I looked it up. It's at-will, both directions. Corinna could let you go tomorrow for basically any reason, and you can walk out the same way. Legally it's clean."

"So then why are you still standing there?"

"Because legal is the floor, not the ceiling." It came out before he could soften it, and Dev looked at him with something between annoyance and curiosity. Luke pushed on. "She's short-handed already. If you vanish on a Saturday, somebody else's night gets wrecked, and that somebody is probably me. But I get that she'd cut you tomorrow if the schedule got tight, and she wouldn't owe you a reason. So it's not like you owe her loyalty. I just don't think the answer is obvious in the direction you want it to be."

Dev stopped wiping. The pretzel warmer ticked as it cooled, and out in the lobby a kid was arguing with his father about whether they'd missed the previews. "You sound like my econ teacher," Dev said. "He'd call that rationalism or something."

"Maybe. But here's the thing I keep going back and forth on. Two weeks from you costs you almost nothing, and it saves a real person a real mess. That math seems simple. And then I think, no, it's not a debt, she never promised you anything, and pretending there's an obligation when there isn't is its own kind of dishonesty." Luke shrugged, palms up. "I can't fully get both of those to fit in my head at once. I'd rather admit that than fake certainty."

Dev was quiet through the next rush, or quiet for Dev, which meant he only complained twice. When the lobby thinned out, he pulled the schedule binder from under the register and turned it to the following month, and Luke watched him study it, chewing the inside of his cheek. "The climbing gym starts me on the fifteenth," Dev said. "If I gave her the tenth through the fifteenth, that's five days. Five days of wearing this visor." He closed the binder, then opened it again, like he was checking whether the days had moved.

At closing, Corinna came through the empty lobby pulling the gates down behind her, and Dev was still standing at the counter with the binder in his hands, thumbing its edge, waiting for her.

story:
The guitar had belonged to Aaron's grandfather, and it came to him through his mother, who carried it into the band room on a Tuesday because he had no car and the case was too long for the bus. It smelled like the inside of a closet, and the strings were dull enough that his reflection in the brass bell of the Sousaphone looked back at him through a fog. He set it on a chair and unlatched the case the way you open something you're not sure you have permission to touch.

His grandfather had played, his mother said, though nobody in the family could say what or how well. The last time anyone remembered hearing it was a wedding fifteen years ago. Aaron had signed up for guitar as his fine arts credit because it was the class that didn't meet before eight in the morning, and because Mr. Reyes let students practice in the band room after school while he sorted sheet music and pretended not to listen.

The problem was the strings. Mr. Reyes had put a page on the board that first week, a diagram Aaron had copied without understanding, and when he pressed his fingers where the page said, the notes came out wrong, soured, like a door that doesn't shut all the way. Priya, who sat near him in class and had been playing since she was nine, leaned over his case one afternoon and frowned at the instrument itself rather than his hands.

"When did you tune it last?" she asked.

"Did I what it?"

She plucked the lowest string, the fat one, and let it wobble out its pitch. "It's not even close. You have to tune it before anything on that page will work." She pointed at the board, where the diagram still hung. "From the lowest string up, it's E, A, D, G, B, and then E again. That's standard tuning." She said it the way she'd tell him the room number for a final, quick, useful, already moving on to her own practice.

He didn't have a tuner. Priya had one, a little green clip, but she was leaving for a lesson, and he wanted, for reasons he couldn't have contextualized without sounding prettier than the truth, to do this part himself. The truth was smaller: he'd watched his grandfather's hands once, at that wedding, before the memory went soft around the edges, and the hands had turned the pegs without looking, the way you adjust a shower you've used for years.

Mr. Reyes kept a pitch pipe in the top drawer of the file cabinet, a thing like a flattened harmonica, and when Aaron asked, he handed it over without a speech. That was the deal with Reyes. He would answer what you asked and then get out of the way, which some students read as indifference and Aaron was beginning to read as respect, a kind of probity about where teaching stopped and your own ear began. Aaron blew into the pipe and got a reedy E, and blew again, and turned the fat string's peg until the two sounds stopped arguing.

The rest went slower. A for the second string, and he learned quickly that the pegs responded differently, one smooth, one gritty, one with a dead spot that needed a nudge past where he thought it should go. D, then G, and by then his fingertips hurt in a specific new way, a striped soreness across the pads. On the fifth string he turned the peg the wrong direction and the pitch climbed away from B, and he had to chase it back down, and this time he counted the turns so he'd know the way back. The thin string worried him most. He'd read enough forum posts at midnight to know it could snap, and he tightened it in small patient fractions until the pipe's high E and the string's high E sat together, not identical, but close enough that the wobble between them slowed like a swing losing momentum.

When all six were there, he played the chord from the page, the one that had sounded like a broken door, and it sounded like a room instead. Not a good room. The guitar had sat in an attic for a decade and its voice had dust in it. But the notes were the right notes, in the right order, and something in his chest went loose and quiet.

Priya found him there an hour later, still in the band room, playing the same four chords over and over because each repetition felt less like an accident. She listened from the doorway for a minute before she came in. "It's flat on the G," she said. "It went out while you were playing. Old guitars do that."

"So I tune it again?"

"So you tune it again. Every time, maybe forever. That's most of it, honestly." She said it without cruelty, the way you tell someone the commute is long. She sat down across from him and took out her own guitar, and for a while they both just tuned, the small clicking of pegs and the thin comparing of pitches filling the band room where the Sousaphone loomed in its corner like a dozing animal.

Aaron thought, while he turned the G back up, that he had spent the year assuming he was the kind of person who didn't stick with things, that this would go the way of the running app and the sourdough starter, and that his grandfather's guitar would end up back in the attic as evidence. He didn't know yet whether that was wrong. But he'd learned something that felt like it could be carried in the hands rather than the head: the instrument didn't hold its tuning on its own, and neither, apparently, did anyone. You came back, you found the E, and you worked up from the lowest string, listening for the wobble to slow.

His stomach growled. Priya laughed without looking up from her pegs, and Aaron checked the high E once more, then closed the case around the guitar, loosely, without snapping the latches all the way, and said, "Same time tomorrow?"

story:
The letter from the art program arrived on a Tuesday, thin enough that Julia knew before opening it that it was a no. They wanted sketches, they had said, five pages from life, and she had sent portraits of her mother at the kitchen table, her brother asleep on the couch, the neighbor's dog tied to the porch rail. Somewhere between the envelope and the recycling bin, her mother rescued it and pinned it to the corkboard, which Julia pretended not to notice.

She decided to apply again, and to do it properly this time, which meant starting over rather than resubmitting the same smudged pages. Her old drawings had a soft, foggy look that she used to think of as atmosphere. Spread across the kitchen table now, they looked like they had been left out in the rain. The shadow under her brother's jaw had drifted down his neck. Her mother's cheekbone had a ghost of itself hovering an inch to the left.

Marcus came over on Thursday with a bag of chips and no plans, the way he had since they were nine. He leaned over the table while she was trying to rescue a portrait, one finger hovering above the paper, not touching. "Which grade did you use?" he asked.

"Grade? It's a pencil."

"They're graded." He picked up the yellow pencil by her elbow and turned it until she could see the letter stamped near the end. "Six B. The soft ones are marked with a B. The more clay in the core, the harder the pencil, and those are marked H. More clay makes a lighter mark. Less clay, more graphite, softer and darker." He set it down. "My dad drafts. I grew up around this stuff."

Julia looked at the pencil as though it had been sitting on her desk for years, which it had. "So everything I drew with this is going to keep smearing."

"Basically, yeah."

She spent Friday evening introspecting in a way she distrusted, lying on her bed cataloguing her own excuses, and decided that honesty was more useful than feeling sorry for herself. The truth was she had never thought about her materials at all. She had thought about faces, about likeness, about the version of her mother she wanted to keep. The paper and the graphite had been as invisible to her as water is to a fish.

Saturday she took the bus to the art store with twenty dollars of birthday money and stood in front of a wall of pencils like a wall of decisions. There were 4H and 2B and HB, whole alphabets of gray. She bought three: a hard one, a middle one, and a soft one, because she wanted to see for herself what the letters actually did. At home she tested them in the back of her notebook, three columns of strokes, and pressed her thumb across each one. The hard pencil left a pale line that barely smudged at all, nearly impermeable to her rubbing finger. The soft one bloomed into a gray smear at the lightest touch. She sat with the notebook open and thought about apportionment, how the same few ingredients, shifted a little one way or the other, made something fixed or something that gave. Her mother came through with laundry, glanced at the columns of strokes, and said nothing, but set a cup of tea down beside them.

The next portrait took two days instead of one afternoon. Julia built her mother's face out of the hard pencil first, pale scaffolding, the cheekbone exactly where it belonged, and only at the end went in with the soft one for the places that were truly dark: the window behind her, the shadow inside her collar. When she finished, she held the page flat and blew across it, and nothing moved. She carried it to the kitchen where Marcus was eating cereal over the sink, a habit she had given up correcting.

He put the bowl down and took the page in both hands. He looked at it for longer than he usually looked at anything.

"So you learned the letters," he said.

"I learned the letters." She took the page back before he could smudge it with his cereal fingers, then, catching herself, held it out again. "Go ahead. Try. Rub the cheekbone."

Marcus pressed his thumb to her mother's face and lifted it clean. Julia laughed, a short, surprised sound, and turned the page to the light.

"That part's a 4H," she said. "The collar's where you'll lose."

activity: the idea of opportunity cost, that choosing one thing means giving up the next best alternative
story:
The envelope from SUNY Purchase sat on the table beside Leo's cold coffee, and under it, face down, was the flyer for Friday's open mic at the Root Cellar, twelve dollars at the door. He had forty-three dollars in his wallet, which was not enough for both the entry fee and the bus ticket his sister had texted him about that morning. Her message was still open on his phone: "Dad's deposition got moved to the 14th, so I'll be in the city overnight. You could crash on my floor, take the 6 a.m. back. Or not. I know money's tight." He read it three times, then turned the flyer over as if the other side might have gotten cheaper.

Across the room, the espresso machine hissed and a barista named Marcus, who wore a faded lunar-lander pin on his apron, argued cheerfully with a woman about a coupon from the mall next door. "Free travel mug for a ten-minute survey," she said, tapping the paper. "Can't beat free." Marcus laughed. "There ain't no such thing as a free lunch," he said, sliding her cup across the counter. "Where'd you get that, a fortune cookie?" "Robert Heinlein," Marcus said. "The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, 1966. He didn't invent it, but that book's the reason everybody says it now."

Leo had come here to do calculus homework, and the torpid warmth of the shop, all steam and sleepy afternoon light, had conspired with his worry until the problem set sat untouched. He copied one derivative, then set down his pencil. Ten minutes for a survey earned a mug, which was maybe eight dollars, which was most of a bus fare. But the ten minutes were the same ten minutes he'd promised to practicing the bridge of his song, the one he'd need if he actually played Friday. He'd been telling himself all week he'd practice tomorrow, and he could feel the plan calcifying into an excuse, tomorrow hardening into a shape he'd never have to act on.

He got in line. The woman with the coupon had gone, and Marcus was wiping the portafilter with the slow care of someone who took small work seriously. "Did you mean that," Leo asked, "about no free lunch?" Marcus shrugged. "I mean the book's good. It's about a moon colony that overthrows Earth. But the saying, yeah. Somebody always pays." He pulled Leo's Americano and, unprompted, nodded at the envelope. "College?" "Deposit's due May first. Three hundred dollars." It came out of him before he'd decided to say it, the way expensive facts do.

Marcus didn't offer him a job or a discount, which Leo half respected him for. He said only, "So what are you giving up to get the three hundred?" and went back to the grounds, their dark deposition settling at the bottom of the tamp like sediment in a riverbed. Leo carried his coffee to the table and sat with the question, which was more use to him than the calculus. The survey mug, the bus ticket, the open mic, the deposit: none of them were free, because each one consumed the same finite wallet, the same finite Friday, the same ten minutes he could only spend once.

He took out his phone and typed to his sister: "I can't come. Money's going to the deposit." He watched the words sit there. What he'd wanted, all along, was not the open mic exactly, but the version of himself who played it; and what he'd lose by skipping it was a night he could picture too clearly, his sister's floor, the early train, the city going by. He thought about adding that, then thought about how it would sound like asking her to talk him out of deciding, and he sent it plain.

Then, because ten minutes is also just ten minutes, he walked next door to the mall kiosk and took the survey anyway. The clipboard asked about laundry detergent and radio habits, and his answers were mostly honest, and at the end the kid behind the counter, maybe nineteen, handed him a travel mug in a plastic sleeve. "Free lunch," the kid said, grinning. "There ain't no such thing," Leo said, and the grin flickered, uncertain whether it had been corrected or complimented. "Robert Heinlein," Leo added. "You'd like it."

He carried the mug back to the coffee shop, where the afternoon crowd had thickened and Marcus was calling out names. His sister had replied with a single thumbs-up, and below it, in the same gray bubble, the address of a diner near her apartment and the words "Saturday, if the deposit clears." He set the mug on his envelope, took out the flyer, and folded it into his pocket instead of throwing it away, pressing it flat against his thigh. Then he picked up his pencil and worked the derivative, and after that the next one, while behind him the machine hissed on.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
story:
Laura had signed up because her guidance counselor said forty hours of volunteering would look good on applications, and because her mother had said, more quietly, that it would be good for her in other ways she'd have to figure out herself. The food bank ran out of the basement of the seniors' residence on Ashrow Street, folding tables stacked with pasta and tins, and on her first Saturday the coordinator handed her a clipboard and a hairnet and told her to greet people at the door.

That was where she met Mrs. Okonjo, who came down from the third floor in a green housecoat and slippers and looked at the tables with an expression Laura couldn't read at first. Not embarrassment, she decided. Something more like appraisal. "You're new," Mrs. Okonjo said. "The last girl stood by the elevator like a security guard. You don't have to do that. Nobody here is going to steal a can of peaches."

Laura laughed, and then a man in a windbreaker took a numbered card from her clipboard and she forgot about the conversation for a while, because there was an actual line, actual people, an old fellow who wanted only soup and a young mother who asked whether the baby formula had an expiry date and Laura had to go check. It had not occurred to her, before Saturday, that a food bank line would contain people who lived in the building itself, upstairs, above the very tables they were queuing for.

During the lull, Mrs. Okonjo settled into a folding chair beside her and asked how old the food bank was. Laura said she didn't know, probably pretty old, and Mrs. Okonjo snorted. "You think so? I remember when there weren't any." She counted on her fingers. "Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981. I was a grown woman already." Laura did the arithmetic twice, because it couldn't be right, and Mrs. Okonjo watched her do it and smiled the way people smile when they've won a small argument with the whole idea of a country.

"Less than fifty years," Laura said. "But before that, what did people do?" Mrs. Okonjo shrugged. "Neighbours, mostly. Or they went hungry quietly." She nodded toward the tables. "My mother would rather have starved than stand in a line where her friends could see her. It stigmatized you, that was the word for it, being known as someone who needed." She said it flatly, a fact about the past rather than a complaint, and then she added that none of this was germane to whether the peaches were good, and demanded Laura open a can for her.

While they ate peaches with plastic forks, a volunteer named Dev, a college student with a laminated map of Canada on the wall, overheard them and admitted he'd assumed food banks had existed since the war. "Some kind of permanent thing," he said. "Like libraries." Mrs. Okonjo said, "We invented libraries before we invented hunger lines, dear. Draw your own conclusions." Laura wrote the date in the margin of her clipboard so she wouldn't lose it, January 16, 1981, and found herself thinking that a thing could be temporary and permanent at once, an emergency that had lasted her whole life and most of her mother's.

At the end of the shift, Dev found a note that had slipped between two crates of juice, and handed it to Laura because she was nearest. It was written in blue ballpoint on the back of a hydro bill envelope, in careful capital letters: "TO WHOEVER RUNS THIS. LAST MONTH I ONLY TOOK HALF MY SHARE BECAUSE A MAN I WENT TO SCHOOL WITH WAS BEHIND ME AND I DIDN'T WANT HIM TO KNOW HOW LITTLE I HAD. THIS MONTH HE WAS NOT THERE SO I TOOK THE REST. PLEASE DON'T PUT THE BEANS IN THE SAME BOX AS THE PET FOOD, IT IS DEPRESSING. THANK YOU FOR THE RICE. IT WAS GOOD RICE."

Laura read it twice, and her eyes were hot by the end of the second reading, and she couldn't have explained why, exactly, except that the good rice part undid her. She looked up at the ceiling, then at the folding tables, then at Mrs. Okonjo, who was back in her chair waiting for someone to walk her to the elevator. Laura crossed the room, took her arm, and pressed the button for three. "It was the middle door," Mrs. Okonjo said, "the good rice. You put it behind the beans where nobody sees it." Laura said she'd move it to the front table, first thing next Saturday, and Mrs. Okonjo said, "Put the peaches beside it."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
Eva had the museum map folded into her back pocket and fifteen minutes before the placement review session started, which was not enough time and was exactly the time she had. She took the escalator two steps at a time to the third floor, where the Hall of Human Biology kept its dim, blue-lit corridor, and found the mitochondria exhibit at the far end, past the plastic brain and the giant walk-in ear.

She had gotten the question wrong on Tuesday. On the practice exam, question forty-one had asked what happens in muscle cells when oxygen runs low, and she had written that lactate builds up as a waste product and shuts the cell down. Her mark came back with a red line through it and a note in the margin: reread fermentation. Daniel, who sat beside her in the review session and had gotten it right, had offered to explain, and she had said no thank you, which had come out colder than she meant. Now it was Saturday, and she was standing in front of a wall display with her phone in her hand, determined to disabuse herself of her own answer before Monday's exam.

The display was called Inside the Powerhouse. A transparent model of a cell the size of a car occupied the middle of the room, its mitochondria picked out in orange. Along the left wall ran a sequence of panels: glucose, glycolysis, pyruvate, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, ATP. She read them in order, resting her fingertips on the railing in front of each one. Glucose split into two molecules of pyruvate, yielding a small payout of ATP. If oxygen was plentiful, the pyruvate went into the mitochondria and the payout grew enormous. If oxygen ran low, the sequence stopped partway, and she stood at that panel for a long time, because the panel stopped partway too. A piece of the interactive screen had gone dark, a recalcitrant gray rectangle where the words about what happened next should have been.

"Are you here for the review session?" a voice asked. A girl of about ten stood beside her, holding a clipboard, a junior docent by her badge. Her badge said Priya.

"No," Eva said. "I'm here to fix my own head. Do you know what this panel says? The one that's out."

Priya looked at the dead rectangle and then at her clipboard. "It's been broken since Thursday. But I know the piece, I had to memorize the script." She read from her clipboard in a flat, rehearsed voice: "When muscle cells run low on oxygen, they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue making 2 ATP per glucose."

"Say that again," Eva said. Priya said it again, slower, and Eva typed it into her phone, then deleted it, because typing it was not the same as having it. "So the lactate isn't the poison. It's the fix."

"It's the trade," Priya said, as though correcting a customer who had misread a price. "You get less ATP that way. Two per glucose. But you keep getting it."

Eva walked to the far wall, where a stationary bike sat in front of a heart-rate monitor, part of an exhibit on exertion. She pedaled hard for ninety seconds, watching her pulse climb and feeling the familiar burn arrive in her thighs, the same burn she had felt in August sprinting across her uncle's farm field to beat a storm to the barn. She had thought then that the burn was the moment her legs gave up. She pedaled and understood that it was the moment her cells improvised. Her legs had kept moving through the whole field, which meant the glycolysis had kept going, which meant the NAD+ had kept coming back, which meant the lactate had been on her side the entire time. She slowed the pedals. A woman waiting behind her with a toddler asked if she was done, and Eva got off, still breathing hard.

She took out her phone to text Daniel. She wrote, I was wrong about forty-one. When muscle cells run low on oxygen they convert pyruvate into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis keeps making 2 ATP per glucose. The lactate isn't what stops you. She looked at the message. It read like the docent's clipboard, flat and complete, and she decided that was fine, because completeness was what she had come for. She sent it.

Daniel replied almost immediately, and his reply was a voice message. She stood under the blue lights with the phone against her ear, sweat cooling on the back of her neck. "Hey," he said. "So first, that's the whole thing, you basically just recited the model answer, nice. Second, I have to tell you something. Professor Ayeni posted an announcement an hour ago. Monday's exam got moved to Friday. Some scheduling thing with the gymnasium." There was a pause with wind in it; he was outside somewhere. "So you spent your Saturday learning this for nothing, kind of."

Eva looked at the broken panel, the gray rectangle that had made her pedal a museum bicycle in front of a toddler to understand a sentence she could have read off a working screen. She thought about the denouement she had been picturing all week: the exam, question forty-one, her pen moving without hesitation, the small private vindication of it. That denouement was gone, or postponed, and the knowledge was still here, sitting in her legs and her phone and her memory, arriving five days early for a party that had been rescheduled.

She put the phone in her pocket and turned back toward the model cell. Priya was leading a family toward the giant ear, clipboard tucked under her arm. Eva caught up with them at the mouth of the walk-in cochlea and tapped the girl on the shoulder.

"Your script," Eva said. "The broken panel. Somebody should tell the front desk it worked anyway."
