activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
story:
Mr. Okafor had taped a sample ballot to the whiteboard on Monday, and by Wednesday it was still there, curling at the corners like a leaf deciding whether to fall. He would not tell them how to vote, he said, but he would not let them treat the election as weather, something that simply happened to the country. "You want to historicize it," he said, tapping the board with a knuckle. "Place it. Ask what came before, what forces arranged it. Then you walk in and pull a lever like you mean it." Mason had written the word in his notebook, historicize, and underlined it twice, though mostly he was thinking about the fact that in nine days he would be eighteen, and in eleven days he would vote.

He had registered in September at the DMV, a trip his grandfather had insisted on driving him to even though the office was four blocks from the school and the weather was still warm. In the car afterward, his grandfather had done the thing he always did at moments he considered ceremonial, turning his wedding ring with his thumb, a mannerism Mason had noticed since he was small and had never asked about. "Nobody in my family voted before 1965," his grandfather said at a red light. "Legally, I mean." He didn't say anything else, and Mason hadn't needed him to.

The morning of the election, Mason woke before his alarm. He ate cereal standing up. He took the sample ballot his teacher had photocopied, folded twice, and put it in his jacket pocket along with his driver's license, and he walked the six blocks to the community hall with his breath showing white in front of him and his stomach doing something complicated that was not quite fear.

The line moved slowly, and he spent it listening to two women behind him argue about a school levy in the polite, murderous way of neighbors. When his turn came, he gave his name to a poll worker with reading glasses on a beaded chain, a woman whose son had been in Mason's chemistry class last year. She ran her finger down the list. Ran it again. Flipped a page, then flipped it back, and Mason felt the paper-thin confidence of the morning begin to go out of him like heat from a cracked window.

"I don't see you here, honey," she said. "Are you sure you're at the right precinct?"

He was sure. He had checked twice. He gave his address, his birthday, the September date of the DMV visit, and she shook her head with real regret, and behind him the line shifted its weight, and Mason's face went hot. He thought of the folded sample ballot in his pocket, of the underlined word in his notebook, of his grandfather turning the ring in a stopped car. He was about to ask whether he could just fill something out, some form, when the woman raised a hand toward a younger poll worker at a side table.

"He can do a provisional ballot," the younger woman said.

"What's that mean," Mason asked, and heard how young his voice came out.

"It's under the Help America Vote Act of 2002," she said. "A voter whose eligibility is in question can cast a provisional ballot. It only counts once officials confirm your eligibility." She handed him a form on a clipboard. "You fill this out, your ballot goes in a special envelope, and if they confirm you're registered, it gets counted."

He filled out the form at the side table, his handwriting smaller and more careful than usual, and fed his ballot into its envelope, and the envelope into a folder, and then there was nothing left to do but thank them and walk out. He told no one at school. When Mr. Okafor asked the class, at the end of fourth period, who had voted that morning, Mason raised his hand, and it did not feel like a lie, exactly, but it did not feel entirely like the truth either, and he held both of those feelings at once without deciding between them, the way you hold two books you intend to read.

The twist came nine days later, in the same classroom, during the same period. Mr. Okafor was collecting essays when the front office called down, and a runner brought Mason a sealed envelope, county stationery, and everyone watched him open it because everyone always watches. The letter said his eligibility had been confirmed. His provisional ballot had been counted. The DMV clerk had simply failed to transmit his registration on time, an oversight, no one's malice, a snag in the nascent machinery of his civic life, now repaired.

That night his grandfather called. "So it counted," he said. "So your vote counted."

"It counted," Mason said. "It just counted late." He was quiet a moment, and then, because his grandfather would understand it in a way no one else would, he added, "The election was called before mine counted. It didn't matter."

"Everything matters," his grandfather said, and Mason heard the ring turn against the phone, a small metallic whisper, once, twice.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
story:
The box had been under the bed in Gran's spare room for as long as Addison could remember, and she had never once been allowed to open it. Tonight Gran had said, almost offhandedly, that she could, which was how Addison knew something had changed, though she did not ask what.

"You're doing that college essay," Gran said from the doorway, hands folded over her cardigan. "The one about family. Take it, then. But read it carefully, not fast."

The box smelled of coal smoke and old paper. Inside were a christening gown gone brown at the hem, a ration book, and a bundle of letters tied with shoelace. Addison untied it on the bed while the light outside went crepuscular and the radiator ticked. The topmost letter was dated 1842, written in a hand so cramped she had to sound the words aloud. A man named Joseph Lockwood, her great-great-great-grandfather, wrote to his sister about shifts at the mill, about the dust that got into his lungs, about being turned off for asking his wage in full. She read it twice. She had expected soldiers or farmers in her family, people who turned up in textbooks. Joseph turned up nowhere.

She carried the letter downstairs. Gran was peeling potatoes at the sink, and the window behind her had gone to purple. Addison read a line aloud, about the foreman docking him a shilling, and Gran set the knife down.

"Your grandfather spent years on that lot," she said. "Before he got ill. He wanted to write it all down, our Joseph and the rest of them, and nobody would take it. Said the library wasn't interested in mill hands." She dried her hands slowly. "There's his study, you know where."

The study still smelled of him, pipe tobacco gone stale in the carpet. Addison found his notebooks first, then, behind them on the low shelf, a battered paperback with a spine cracked white. The Making of the English Working Class. 1963, said the title page, and E. P. Thompson. In the margin, in her grandfather's pencil, a line was underlined twice: he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from, and then in quotes, the enormous condescension of posterity. She did not know the word posterity at first, then she did: everyone who came after, everyone like her. She sat down on the floor with the book in her lap and the notebook open beside her and did not notice the room going dark.

Her grandfather's notes were the problem. In one notebook he had written that Joseph was out on strike in 1842, standing with the hands. In the other, later notebook, the claim had a question mark beside it, and a page reference to a newspaper of the time that listed Joseph Lockwood among the men who went back in on the third day. Addison went back and forth between the two notebooks, then to the letters, then to the book. The newspaper was a partial thing, she understood; its owner hated the strikers, and a list in such a paper could be wrong, or vindictive. But the first notebook rested on a story Joseph's daughter had told sixty years after the fact, which was partial too, the apportionment of blame smoothed by family love. She could not predicate Joseph's loyalty on either source alone, and she could not stop wanting to know it.

She carried both notebooks down to the kitchen. "Gran, which one is true? Was he out on strike or wasn't he?"

Gran looked at the pencil question mark for a long moment. "I never asked him," she said. "He'd sit there with his papers and I'd think, there's tea to be made. I never asked what he'd found." She tapped the page. "Maybe he couldn't decide either. That's why the question mark."

The potatoes were boiling over. Gran lifted the pan and Addison found herself holding both notebooks against her chest, the way you hold something you're afraid of being asked to put down. She thought about her grandfather, alone in this room, wanting to rescue a man no book had room for, and ending on a question mark anyway. She would write the essay with both versions in it. She would say what she could not settle.

"The enormous condescension of posterity," she said aloud, testing it.

"What's that, love?"

"Nothing. Something Grandad underlined." She set the notebooks on the table, side by side, question mark facing up, and reached for a plate.

story:
The math club met on Thursdays in the back corner of the school library, at the two tables nearest the window where the afternoon light came in flat and gold across the scratched wood. Keira arrived early, as she usually did, and spread out her binder, the problem set from Tuesday still unfinished. The problem asked for the area enclosed between a line and a parabola, and she had gotten an answer she did not believe, because it was negative, and an area, she was fairly sure, could not be.

"I got forty-one over six," said Devon, dropping into the chair across from her and sliding his notebook over so she could see. His work was neat, almost architectural, each step ruled off from the next with a straight edge.

"I got the same number," Keira said. "Negative forty-one over six."

Devon frowned at her page, then at his. Priya came over from the shelves with a book on typography she had been carrying around for a week, set it down, and looked at both solutions. "You integrated the same things," she said. "Look. Same functions, same limits. He did parabola minus line. You did line minus parabola."

"Then which one is the area?" Keira asked. Nobody answered right away. Somewhere near the circulation desk a scanner beeped, twice, and the librarian murmured something to a freshman about a late fee, a small disbursement of quarters counted out onto the counter. Keira listened to the coins without looking up, her pencil resting on the margin where she had been doodling the two curves.

She had drawn them before she ever computed anything; that was how she liked to start, sketch first, numbers second. On her page the line cut through the parabola, and between the two crossing points the parabola rode above the line, a closed sliver of shaded region, thin at the ends and fat in the middle. She shaded it lightly with the side of her pencil, then held the page up so the others could see. "The parabola's the upper one," she said. "The whole way across, between where they cross. It's on top."

"So the area is the integral of the upper function minus the lower function," Priya said slowly, reading the picture as much as the symbols. "Over the interval where they're ordered that way. Parabola minus line. That's Devon's."

Keira looked at her own negative answer, then at Devon's positive one, and felt the two halves of her brain settle into their usual argument. The part of her that trusted procedure wanted a rule she could apply blindly, write once in her notes and never question: bigger minus smaller, done. The part of her that trusted the picture distrusted any rule that worked without looking, because a parabola and a line could cross again somewhere outside the interval, could trade places, and then a single memorized subtraction would fail her. The rule was not really about parabolas or lines at all, she realized. It was about which function was above which, over a specific stretch.

"Try it backwards," she said to Devon. "Draw your curves first. Don't compute anything, just draw."

Devon, who never drew anything if he could avoid it, took out a fresh sheet and sketched the parabola opening upward, then the line slicing through it. He shaded the sliver between the crossing points, his hand less certain than hers but the shape unmistakable. "It's the same picture," he said, sounding almost betrayed by his own arithmetic. "I just got lucky with the order."

"Not lucky," Priya said. "You did upper minus lower. You just didn't check that it was upper."

Keira tried a second problem, one she invented on the spot, where the line rode above a downward-opening parabola, and made herself find which was upper before she touched a single integral. Then a third where the two curves crossed inside her interval, just to see what would break, and something did break, the shaded region flipping sides halfway through, and she sat with that for a moment, her pencil still, the inchoate shape of a harder idea forming at the edge of her attention. She would have to split the interval, she thought, at the crossing point, and handle each piece separately. She was not sure yet. She wrote a question mark beside it instead of an answer.

She thought about how easily she could have imputed the difference between her answer and Devon's to carelessness, hers or his, some slipped sign or dropped term, and gone on to the next problem knowing nothing. Instead the wrongness had been the whole lesson. The sign had been telling her something true: that she had measured the region from underneath.

"Forty-one over six," she said, and wrote it at the bottom of the page with the units, square units, in small letters after the fraction. Then she turned the page over, drew two new curves crossing twice, and slid the sheet across the table to Devon. "Your turn. Don't compute yet. Shade it."

story:
The restaurant smelled like burnt coffee and maple syrup, a combination Samuel would later associate with the entire summer he turned sixteen. He sat at the corner table of the Ridgeview Diner with his hands folded, the way his mother had told him to, while the manager, a reticent man named Delgado who spoke mostly in short declarative sentences, looked over his one-page application.

"You're sixteen," Delgado said. It wasn't a question, so Samuel didn't answer it. "Weekends, bussing tables, clearing plates, restocking. Seven twenty-five an hour." He said the number the way he said everything, flat, as though it had been posted on the wall for years, which in a sense it had.

Samuel had prepared a few things to say, mostly about his work ethic, but the number caught him off guard. It sounded small. It sounded like the price of two and a half milkshakes at the restaurant he was sitting in. He said yes anyway, because a job was a job, and because his friend Marcus had been teasing him for weeks about being the last of their group without one.

That evening Marcus came over, and they sat on the porch steps while the sprinklers hissed across the lawn. Marcus had started two weeks earlier at a burger place one town over, and he was still in the flush of it, showing Samuel his first paycheck like a winning lottery ticket. Then he paused, squinting at it. "Wait. Yours will be seven twenty-five? I make more than that. Like, more per hour."

"How much more?" Samuel asked.

"Enough that it's weird. We do the same stuff. You're not worse at carrying plates than I am at carrying trays." Marcus turned the stub over as though the explanation might be printed on the back. "It's not like you're worse at anything."

Samuel thought of his geometry teacher, Mr. Okonkwo, who had a habit of saying that before you solve a problem you have to agree on what kind of problem it is. Some things were exercises, some were theorems, and some were what he called lemmas, smaller results you needed first, the scaffolding under the real proof. Samuel had liked that idea, the notion that you could be honest about not yet knowing something, that uncertainty was a station you could work from rather than a failure.

He looked it up on his phone while Marcus ate the last of the pretzels. The federal minimum wage was $7.25 an hour, and it had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, which meant it had been the same number since Samuel was in preschool. But many states and cities set a higher minimum, and Marcus's burger place sat just across the state line, in a state that had done exactly that. Samuel read the dates twice. He thought about 2009, about how his parents talked about that year, and about how a number could sit still for so long while everything around it moved.

"So it's not the boss being cheap," Marcus said, leaning over to see the screen. "It's the law. Different law here."

"Here it's the federal one. There it's the state one." Samuel turned the phone off and set it face down on the step, the way Mr. Okonkwo did when he wanted a class to think instead of read.

Marcus left after that, satisfied, but Samuel stayed on the steps until the sprinklers shut off. He found himself weighing something he couldn't quite name. Part of him thought he should quit before he started and apply across the line, where the same hours would add up to more, and part of him thought that was a cowardly way to think about the diner, about Delgado, about the town he'd grown up in. His grandfather had worked at the hardware store on Miller Road for forty-one years and had never once, as far as Samuel knew, compared his pay to anyone else's. Samuel admired that and also suspected it was a kind of surrender, a willingness to let habit subjugate ambition and call the result loyalty. He could not decide which interpretation was fair, or whether fairness had anything to do with it.

The next morning, a Saturday, he took the bus to the diner for his first shift. Delgado handed him a tan apron and a rag and pointed at table eleven, where a family of five had just left a wreckage of napkins and half-eaten pancakes. Samuel tied the apron, gathered the plates with the careful stacking motion he'd practiced in his mirror at home, and carried them toward the kitchen. Behind him he heard Delgado say, without looking up from the register, "Bus fourteen next. And smile at the door when you pass it."

Samuel adjusted his grip on the plates, caught his own reflection in the chrome panel by the pass-through window, and smiled.

story:
The fourth floor vending machine took Sadie's dollar and gave nothing back, which felt like the whole week in miniature. She had spent Tuesday in Mr. Okafor's seminar arguing about a pesticide called Kelvar with a boy named Dmitri, and she was still losing the argument in her head three days later, on the teal upholstered chair outside room 412, where she was supposed to be delivering a water pitcher.

Dmitri had leaned back and said the burden of proof lay with the people claiming harm, that you waited for evidence before you banned something, because bans cost jobs. Sadie had wanted to argue and found she couldn't, not cleanly, not the way she could argue about things she'd actually read. So she'd gone home and typed serious irreversible damage into the library search bar at midnight, and the phrase had surfaced a document she'd never heard of, and now she had it screenshotted on her phone like a stone in her pocket.

The water pitcher was for Mr. Ahmadi, who had a liver thing nobody on the floor said out loud and a daughter named Layla who came every evening at six with a canvas bag of hospital-inappropriate food. Sadie had learned the shift's geography in three weeks: which nurses wanted silence, which families wanted talking, which rooms you knocked on twice and which you passed quickly. The Ahmadi room was a talking room. Layla was maybe twenty-five, worked in county public health, and treated Sadie like a person rather than a polo shirt.

"You look like you're studying for something," Layla said today, catching her refilling the pitcher. "Or against something."

"A debate I already lost." Sadie set the pitcher down. "There's this pesticide they want to use near the river, and I said we should hold off, and this guy said, wait for proof it actually hurts people. And I didn't have an answer. I had a feeling and no answer."

Mr. Ahmadi turned his head toward the window. Layla smiled at him, then back at Sadie. "My whole job is that argument. Do you know the Rio Declaration?"

Sadie shook her head, feeling the screenshot grow warm in her pocket.

"Nineteen ninety-two, big UN environment meeting. Principle fifteen." Layla pulled a tab on her coffee lid, unhurried. "It says where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay cost-effective preventive measures. People call it the precautionary principle."

"That's a mouthful."

"It's a leash," Layla said. "It keeps 'we're not sure yet' from becoming 'never.'"

Sadie took out her phone and found the screenshot and held it up, and Layla laughed, short and surprised, and said, "You already had it. Why are you losing to this boy?"

Because, Sadie admitted, it felt like the principle cut both ways, and she said so, pulling the visitor chair closer. If you acted without certainty, you could ruin livelihoods over nothing; if you waited, you ruined a river you couldn't un-ruin. Irreversible was doing a lot of work in that sentence, and so was cost-effective, and she suspected Dmitri would grab both words and pull. Layla listened with her chin on her fist and offered nothing, which Sadie was beginning to understand was how Layla talked best.

"There was a case in my office," Layla said finally, quietly, glancing at her father. "A well near a plant. Kids with the same bloodwork, more or less. The company's experts said causality was equivocal, too many other explanations, no proof the plant did it. And they were right, technically. Proof takes years. The families had months." She straightened the blanket edge without seeming to notice she'd done it. "The county couldn't make the plant close on suspicion. But they could require testing the town had to pay for, and they did, and the testing came back worse than anyone guessed. Nobody was absolved, exactly. Everyone had done the defensible thing."

"And the kids?"

"Some of them are fine. It's not a story with a shape." Layla gathered her canvas bag, checking the time. "Tell your Dmitri the principle doesn't say who's right. It says who has to move first."

Sadie walked the empty pitcher back down the corridor, past the vending machine she now forgave, past a nurse dictating notes in a low monotone, and thought about the word defensible, which she hadn't used before tonight and which she disliked on contact. Outside room 409 an old woman waved her over to fix a window blind that had stuck halfway, admitting gray evening light at a crooked angle, and Sadie stood on a chair and worked the mechanism until it gave. The blind snapped down all the way, darker than the room needed, and the old woman said, "Oh, well, now I can't see the parking lot at all," and laughed, and Sadie stood there with her hand still on the cord, deciding whether to raise it again.

story:
The rink smelled like cold rubber and burnt coffee, and the party had taken over the benches behind the boards, where Loic's aunts had laid out a table of noodle boxes that were going lukewarm while everyone watched the screen above the skate rental counter. On the ice, his little cousin's skating lesson was winding down, but nobody was watching the ice. The big screen was showing the World Cup match, and the sound was off, which somehow made everyone louder.

"Forty-eight," said Théo, Loic's cousin, holding a fork like a gavel. "I'm telling you, this one has forty-eight teams. It's the first time ever."

"It's thirty-two," said Uncle Marcel. "It's always been thirty-two. You're inventing things." He reached across Loic for a spring roll. "More teams means worse teams. Dilution. Like adding water to good soup."

Loic had been quiet, working through his own disagreement with himself. He liked Uncle Marcel's argument; it had the shape of something true, a preference for excellence over inclusion. But he also remembered something Théo's numbers were brushing against, something about the tournament being different this time, bigger, stranger. He couldn't place where he'd learned it, which bothered him, because a fact you can't place is a fact you shouldn't use.

"You're both guessing," he said, and pulled out his phone.

"Look at this," Uncle Marcel said, gesturing at the screen with his fork. "The match is in Toronto. The next one, my friend at work says, is in Mexico City. How does a tournament travel like that? It's absurd. A proper tournament has one host, one crowd, one heartbeat."

Loic scrolled. The wifi at the rink was friable, thin as old ice, and the page loaded in pieces: first the year, 2026, then a headline, then the sentence he'd been half-remembering. He read it twice, feeling the small satisfaction of a thing settling into place.

"It's forty-eight," he said. "This World Cup, 2026. First one ever with forty-eight teams. And it's hosted by three countries." He looked up. "Canada, Mexico, and the United States. That's the whole thing. First with forty-eight, first with three hosts."

Théo put down his fork with the gravity of a judge. "I said forty-eight."

"You said forty-eight and invented a reason," Loic said. "Different crime."

The aunts laughed. Uncle Marcel waved him off, but he leaned in to see the screen, and Loic let him read it himself rather than disabusing him out loud, because a man who finds his own error keeps more dignity than one who is corrected in front of spring rolls.

"But Marcel has a point," Loic went on, surprising himself by saying it, since he'd spent most of the argument against him. "Sort of. I think." Everyone turned back to him, and he felt the pressure of having to sound surer than he was. "More teams probably means more bad matches early on. That's just arithmetic. But it also means more countries get to be in it, whole places that never qualified before, kids watching who've never seen their flag in a tournament. That's worth something. I don't know which thing matters more. Maybe they both do."

"That's not a position," Théo said. "That's a shrug with vocabulary."

"It's a position with an asterisk," Loic said. "I'm allowed the asterisk."

Down the glass, the birthday girl came off the ice, blades hissing on the last dry strip before the door, cheeks red as stop signs, helmet crooked. She barrelled into the row of coats and Loic caught her, mostly, one skate blade scraping his shin on the way past. On the screen above them, the muted crowd in Toronto rose as one, a wave of blue and green, and here in the rink the whole family rose with it, shouting at a television with no sound, and Uncle Marcel was shouting loudest of all.

"See," he said, pointing at the screen as the ball hit the net. "Forty-eight teams and still only one can win it. That part I like."

Loic's little cousin tugged his sleeve and asked him who he was cheering for, and he honestly did not know yet. "The host countries," he said. "All three. It's their party." She considered this, and skated a slow circle around the bench to show it was acceptable.

Behind the counter, the rental clerk turned the volume up, and the noise of the crowd came through at last, and it was louder than all of them.

story:
Carter had promised himself he would finish the physics problem set before dinner, and now the sun was going down over the fence and he had finished exactly one problem, which he had finished wrong. He sat at the picnic table with the textbook propped against a jar of nails, his pencil chewed to splinters, and tried again to make the numbers behave. The problem was about a ball launched off a table at some horizontal speed, and the book kept insisting, in its bland way, that he separate the motion into components, as if velocity were a bag of mixed nuts he could sort into bowls.

He understood the idea and did not believe it. That was the uncomfortable part. The equations said that the ball's sideways speed had nothing to do with how fast it fell, that the vertical part went about its business as if the horizontal part didn't exist, and every instinct he had said a ball thrown hard ought to hang in the air longer than a ball simply tipped off the edge. His uncle, a man who could fix a transmission and quote Kierkegaard in the same breath and called himself a polymath mostly at cookouts, had told him once that physics was mostly learning to distrust your eyes. Carter had thought that sounded profound at the time. Now it sounded like an excuse.

Priya came through the back gate carrying two tennis balls and a bag of chips she had clearly already started, because she was loquacious when she was eating and she was already talking. "Your mom said you were being tragic back here. I brought props."

"I'm not tragic. I'm stuck."

She dropped onto the bench across from him and read the problem upside down, which she claimed she was good at and was not. "A ball rolls off a table at four meters per second. Blah blah. Where does it land." She tossed one tennis ball in the air and caught it. "You know what I think? I think you're overcomplicating it because it feels too easy."

"That's the thing. It doesn't feel easy. It feels wrong."

"Then don't feel it. Test it." She stood up and put one ball on the table's edge, holding it with one finger, and held the other in her other hand. "Okay. Bet. This one I just drop. This one I throw straight out, level, as hard as I can. Same height, same second. Which one hits the grass first?"

"The dropped one," Carter said immediately. "The thrown one's in the air longer. It's traveling farther, so it takes longer to come down."

"Fifty cents."

"You're on."

Here is what Priya would remember about it afterward: the way he said it, absolutely certain, like a man announcing his own birthday. She counted down from three, dropped the one finger and snapped the other wrist at the same instant, and both of them froze, heads tilted, listening. The two sounds came so close together that she honestly could not have sworn to the order, so they did it again, and then a third time, and on the third time she made him be the one to throw so she could only listen, eyes shut, chips forgotten in her hand.

"They hit together," Carter said.

"Say it properly."

"One sound. They hit the grass at the same time." He said it twice more, as though the sentence might change under repetition. The thrown ball had sailed a good four meters and the dropped one had landed practically at the table's leg, and they had landed together, and somewhere in his chest a door swung open onto a room he hadn't known was there. The book wasn't sorting mixed nuts. The book was saying you could let two things be true at once, that the fall and the flight were separate and simultaneous, that the problem had two lives running side by side and you were allowed to look at them one at a time.

He went back to the picnic table and did the problem in four minutes. The horizontal part was just distance equals rate times time, a thing he had known since seventh grade. The vertical part was free fall, which he had done last week. What had seemed like one impossible braided thing turned out to be two easy things refusing to touch each other, and he wondered whether that was a trick of physics or a way of seeing you could subsume other problems under, though he wasn't sure yet and wasn't going to pretend to be. Some problems probably really were braided all the way through. This one, gloriously, was not.

"Four point two meters," he said.

"From the table?"

"From the table's edge. Four point two meters out." He held up the paper. "And I only believe it because of your fifty cents, which you still owe me, by the way, since I lost the bet and you never actually paid up either direction."

Priya dug in her pocket, produced two quarters, and set them on the table next to the jar of nails, where they sat catching the last of the light. "For the record," she said, "I only bet against you because you sounded too sure." She tossed him the second tennis ball. "Throw it again. I want to hear it one more time."

story:
The summer league practiced on the ragged field behind the community center, where the goals had holes and the water fountain only worked if you hit it on its left side. Alexia had joined because her roommate at State had said it would be easy, and it was, at first. Nobody counted anything. The team lost 4-1, then 6-2, and at practice on Thursday half the girls walked through the shuttle drill while Coach Reyes stacked cones with the resignation of a woman who had seen this before.

"Can I try something?" Alexia asked her afterward, while the others filed toward the parking lot. She'd found a stopwatch app on her phone during her statistics lecture that spring, half-listening, and the idea had sat in her since. "If we timed everyone's sprints separately. Like, each person gets her own number, posted on the fence."

Coach Reyes looked at her for a long moment. "You want to be the one holding the stopwatch? That's a popularity contest you'll lose."

"I know," Alexia said. "But everybody walking isn't working either."

The stopwatch came out on Monday. She called out times as each girl finished the forty-yard sprint, and Priya, who played midfield and never lifted above a jog in drills, glanced at the fence where Alexia had taped a sheet of paper with everyone's name on it. Priya's time was second-worst. On the second sprint she beat two people. By the third round, girls who usually saved themselves for games were spitting into the grass and putting hands on knees, and the sheet of paper on the fence had numbers nobody wanted next to their name.

"You know there's a name for this," Priya said afterward, wringing out her shirt. "My brother's taking psych at City. He says it's called social loafing. People slack in groups, and the slacking shrinks when each person's contribution can be identified." She shrugged. "I didn't believe him until I saw my own time up there."

Alexia wrote the times down every practice after that, and the team's losses narrowed. But it wasn't clean. Dana, their sweeper, who had organized carpools all June and once drove forty minutes to bring Cleo shin guards she'd forgotten, stopped carpooling. She'd pulled a hamstring in the third timed session and played through it badly rather than have a slow number posted, and when Alexia asked if she was okay, Dana said, "You'd write it down, wouldn't you," and walked to her car alone.

Alexia sat on the bleachers that night trying to interpolate between two things she believed. If she charted the averages, effort had clearly risen across the squad; the numbers were unambiguous. What the numbers didn't capture was Dana driving alone, or the way girls now paired off for water breaks instead of collapsing in one sweating heap the way they had in June. She kept running the comparison and it kept sliding: more effort, less team, and no stopwatch in the world that measured the second thing.

She brought it to Priya during a scrimmage break, both of them lying in the shade of the one good tree. "I don't think the times are the point anymore," Alexia said. "I think the point is that we're fifteen individuals now. We happen to wear the same shirt."

"Individuals who run hard," Priya said. "In June we were a group that jogged."

"That's the whole trade, though. That's it, exactly. Group and slow, or separate and fast."

Priya picked at the grass. "My brother would say you can't have it both ways. Accountability breaks the loafing apart, and it breaks other stuff apart too."

The semifinal was the following Saturday, and Alexia made a decision she couldn't fully defend. She timed the sprints as always, but after practice she pulled Dana aside by the fountain, smacked its left side with the heel of her hand, and said, "You don't go on the sheet till the hamstring's healed. Your time stays whatever it was before." Dana studied her, waiting for the catch. "That's not fair to everyone else," Dana said finally, and Alexia said, "I know. I can't tell if it's the right kind of unfair." She meant it. The sprint numbers had risen the whole season and she could not prove that the numbers had caused it, that it wasn't August pride or Dana's bad example or just girls getting fit; and now she was carving an exception out of the one system that had worked, on a hunch that a team was a thing the numbers could kill.

They lost the semifinal 2-1, on a goal that slid through the exact gap Dana would have closed. She'd played the whole second half on the bad leg, refusing to come off, and afterward she sat with her shin packed in ice while the others gathered around the schedule to see when the third-place game was.

Dana waved Alexia over. "My time tomorrow," she said. "Put it on the sheet."
